concepts.title: Kinetic Theory of Temperature and Pressure
concepts.content_html:
Kinetic Theory of Temperature and Pressure

When you inflate a bicycle tire on a hot day, the tire feels firmer than on a cold morning — even though you pumped in the same amount of air. The reason lies in the kinetic theory of gases, which connects the invisible motion of billions of molecules to the temperature and pressure we can measure.

The Kinetic Molecular Model

An ideal gas is modeled as a large number of tiny particles (atoms or molecules) in constant, random motion. Key assumptions:

  • Gas particles are point-like — their volume is negligible compared to the container.
  • Collisions between particles and with container walls are perfectly elastic (kinetic energy is conserved).
  • There are no attractive or repulsive forces between particles (except during collisions).
  • The average kinetic energy of the particles depends only on the absolute temperature.

Temperature and Kinetic Energy

Temperature is a macroscopic measure of the average translational kinetic energy of gas molecules:

\[ K_{\text{avg}} = \frac{3}{2} k_B T \]

where:

  • \( K_{\text{avg}} \) = average translational kinetic energy per molecule (J)
  • \( k_B = 1.38 \times 10^{-23} \) J/K = Boltzmann constant
  • \( T \) = absolute temperature (K)

This means doubling the Kelvin temperature doubles the average kinetic energy of the molecules.

Root-Mean-Square Speed

The rms (root-mean-square) speed of gas molecules relates to temperature and molecular mass:

\[ v_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{\frac{3 k_B T}{m}} \]

where \( m \) is the mass of one molecule. Lighter molecules move faster at the same temperature.

Pressure from Molecular Collisions

Gas pressure arises from the collective force of molecules bouncing off container walls. More frequent and harder collisions mean higher pressure. Pressure depends on:

  • Number density of molecules (\( N/V \))
  • Average kinetic energy (which depends on \( T \))

\[ P = \frac{N}{V} \cdot \frac{1}{3} m v_{\text{rms}}^2 = \frac{2}{3} \frac{N}{V} K_{\text{avg}} \]

Key Idea: Temperature is not a measure of heat — it is a measure of the average kinetic energy of molecules. Two objects at the same temperature have molecules with the same average kinetic energy, regardless of size or material.
AP Exam Tip: Always use Kelvin for temperature in kinetic theory equations. To convert: \( T(K) = T(°C) + 273 \). The AP exam will often test whether you recognize that absolute zero (0 K) corresponds to zero molecular kinetic energy.

problem_sets.title: Practice: Kinetic Theory of Temperature and Pressure

problems.question_html: According to kinetic theory, the temperature of an ideal gas is directly proportional to which of the following?

choices.text: The number of molecules in the gas
The average translational kinetic energy of the molecules
The total mass of the gas

hints.text: Think about the equation that relates temperature to molecular motion.
\( K_{\text{avg}} = \frac{3}{2} k_B T \) — temperature is proportional to average kinetic energy.

solution_steps.text: The kinetic theory equation \( K_{\text{avg}} = \frac{3}{2} k_B T \) shows that temperature is directly proportional to the average translational kinetic energy of molecules.
Temperature does not depend on the number of molecules, volume, or total mass — only on how fast the molecules are moving on average.

problems.question_html: Two containers hold the same ideal gas at the same temperature. Container A has twice the volume of Container B but the same number of molecules. Which container has the higher pressure?

choices.text: Cannot be determined without knowing the molecular mass

hints.text: Pressure depends on how often molecules hit the walls. How does volume affect collision frequency?
\( P = \frac{2}{3} \frac{N}{V} K_{\text{avg}} \). Same \( N \) and \( T \), but Container B has half the volume, so its \( N/V \) is larger.

solution_steps.text: Since both containers have the same temperature, molecules have the same average kinetic energy.
Pressure depends on number density \( N/V \). Container B has the same \( N \) in half the volume, so \( N/V \) is twice as large.
Therefore Container B has twice the pressure.

problems.question_html: The temperature of an ideal gas is increased from 200 K to 400 K. By what factor does the average translational kinetic energy of the molecules change?

hints.text: Average kinetic energy is directly proportional to absolute temperature.
\( K_{\text{avg}} \propto T \). If \( T \) doubles (200 K → 400 K), then \( K_{\text{avg}} \) doubles.

solution_steps.text: From \( K_{\text{avg}} = \frac{3}{2} k_B T \), kinetic energy is proportional to \( T \).

problems.question_html: At 300 K, what is the average translational kinetic energy of a single gas molecule? Use \( k_B = 1.38 \times 10^{-23} \) J/K. Give your answer in units of \( 10^{-21} \) J, rounded to two decimal places.

hints.text: Use \( K_{\text{avg}} = \frac{3}{2} k_B T \).

problem_sets.title: Premium: Kinetic Theory of Temperature and Pressure

problems.question_html: Oxygen (\( O_2 \), molar mass 32 g/mol) and hydrogen (\( H_2 \), molar mass 2 g/mol) are at the same temperature. What is the ratio \( v_{\text{rms, H}_2} / v_{\text{rms, O}_2} \)?

hints.text: The rms speed depends on mass: \( v_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{3k_BT/m} \). At the same \( T \), how does the ratio depend on \( m \)?
\( \frac{v_{\text{rms, H}_2}}{v_{\text{rms, O}_2}} = \sqrt{\frac{m_{O_2}}{m_{H_2}}} = \sqrt{\frac{32}{2}} = \sqrt{16} = 4 \).

solution_steps.text: Hydrogen molecules move 4 times faster than oxygen molecules at the same temperature.

problems.question_html: A gas at 27°C has an rms speed of 500 m/s. If the temperature is raised to 927°C, what is the new rms speed in m/s?

hints.text: First convert to Kelvin. Then use \( v_{\text{rms}} \propto \sqrt{T} \).

concepts.title: The Ideal Gas Law
concepts.content_html:
The Ideal Gas Law

From weather balloons expanding as they rise to the warning on aerosol cans about heating, the ideal gas law governs how gases behave when pressure, volume, and temperature change.

The Equation

The ideal gas law combines several earlier gas laws (Boyle's, Charles's, Avogadro's) into one equation:

\[ PV = nRT \]

where:

  • \( P \) = pressure (Pa)
  • \( V \) = volume (m\(^3\))
  • \( n \) = number of moles
  • \( R = 8.314 \) J/(mol·K) = universal gas constant
  • \( T \) = absolute temperature (K)

Alternatively, using the number of molecules \( N \) and Boltzmann's constant:

\[ PV = Nk_BT \]

where \( N = nN_A \) and \( k_B = R/N_A = 1.38 \times 10^{-23} \) J/K.

Special Cases

When one variable is held constant:

  • Boyle's Law (constant \( T \) and \( n \)): \( P_1V_1 = P_2V_2 \) — pressure and volume are inversely proportional.
  • Charles's Law (constant \( P \) and \( n \)): \( V_1/T_1 = V_2/T_2 \) — volume and temperature are directly proportional.
  • Gay-Lussac's Law (constant \( V \) and \( n \)): \( P_1/T_1 = P_2/T_2 \) — pressure and temperature are directly proportional.

Worked Example

A balloon contains 0.50 mol of helium at 1.0 atm and 300 K. What is the volume?

\[ V = \frac{nRT}{P} = \frac{(0.50)(8.314)(300)}{1.013 \times 10^5} = 0.0123 \text{ m}^3 \approx 12.3 \text{ L} \]

Key Idea: The ideal gas law assumes no intermolecular forces and negligible molecular volume. It works best at low pressures and high temperatures where these assumptions are most valid.
AP Exam Tip: Watch your units! Pressure must be in Pa and volume in m\(^3\) when using \( R = 8.314 \) J/(mol·K). If given kPa, atm, or liters, convert first. The combined gas law \( \frac{P_1V_1}{T_1} = \frac{P_2V_2}{T_2} \) is a useful shortcut when \( n \) is constant.

problems.question_html: A fixed amount of ideal gas is in a sealed container. If the temperature is doubled while the volume remains constant, what happens to the pressure?

hints.text: With constant \( V \) and \( n \), use Gay-Lussac's Law.
\( P \propto T \) when \( V \) is constant. Doubling \( T \) doubles \( P \).

solution_steps.text: From \( PV = nRT \) with constant \( V \) and \( n \): \( P \propto T \).
Doubling the temperature doubles the pressure.

problems.question_html: An ideal gas at 2.0 atm occupies 4.0 L. If the gas is compressed isothermally to 1.0 L, what is the new pressure in atm?

hints.text: Isothermal means constant temperature. Use Boyle's Law.

problems.question_html: A gas occupies 3.0 L at 300 K. If the pressure is kept constant and the temperature is raised to 600 K, what is the new volume in liters?

hints.text: At constant pressure, \( V \propto T \) (Charles's Law).

problems.question_html: How many moles of an ideal gas are contained in a 0.020 m\(^3\) container at 1.013 \(\times 10^5\) Pa and 400 K? Use \( R = 8.314 \) J/(mol·K). Round to two decimal places.

hints.text: Rearrange \( PV = nRT \) to solve for \( n \).

problems.question_html: A sealed rigid container holds an ideal gas at 1.5 atm and 27°C. The gas is heated until the pressure reaches 3.0 atm. What is the final temperature in °C?

hints.text: Rigid container means constant volume. Use \( P_1/T_1 = P_2/T_2 \) in Kelvin.

solution_steps.text: Convert: \( T_1 = 27 + 273 = 300 \) K. Constant volume: \( P/T = \text{const} \).

problems.question_html: A weather balloon with a volume of 1.0 m\(^3\) is released at sea level (\( P = 1.0 \times 10^5 \) Pa, \( T = 300 \) K). At a certain altitude the pressure is \( 5.0 \times 10^4 \) Pa and the temperature is 250 K. What is the volume of the balloon at that altitude, in m\(^3\)? Round to one decimal place.

hints.text: Use the combined gas law: \( \frac{P_1V_1}{T_1} = \frac{P_2V_2}{T_2} \).
\( V_2 = V_1 \times \frac{P_1}{P_2} \times \frac{T_2}{T_1} = 1.0 \times \frac{1.0 \times 10^5}{5.0 \times 10^4} \times \frac{250}{300} \approx 1.7 \) m\(^3\).

problems.question_html: An ideal gas in a cylinder with a movable piston undergoes an isobaric expansion. The initial volume is 2.0 L at 350 K. If the volume increases to 5.0 L, what is the final temperature in K?

hints.text: Isobaric means constant pressure. Use Charles's Law.

problems.question_html: A rigid container holds 2.0 mol of an ideal gas at 400 K. The gas exerts a pressure of \( 3.0 \times 10^5 \) Pa. Determine the volume of the container in m\(^3\). Use \( R = 8.314 \) J/(mol·K). Express your answer and explain how the ideal gas law applies.
problems.sample_answer: Using PV = nRT: V = nRT/P = (2.0)(8.314)(400) / (3.0 × 10^5) = 6651.2 / 300000 = 0.0222 m³ ≈ 0.022 m³. The ideal gas law relates pressure, volume, temperature, and amount of gas. Since the container is rigid, V is fixed, and increasing T would increase P proportionally.
rubric: Correctly applies PV = nRT and solves for V (1 point)
Correct numerical answer with appropriate units: V ≈ 0.022 m³ (1 point)
Explains the relationship between variables and the constraint of a rigid container (1 point)

hints.text: Rearrange the ideal gas law to solve for volume.

solution_steps.text: The ideal gas law shows that for a fixed amount of gas, if the container is rigid (\( V \) constant), then \( P \propto T \).

problems.correct_answer: Using PV = nRT: V = nRT/P = (2.0)(8.314)(400) / (3.0 × 10^5) = 6651.2 / 300000 = 0.0222 m³ ≈ 0.022 m³. The ideal gas law relates pressure, volume, temperature, and amount of gas. Since the container is rigid, V is fixed, and increasing T would increase P proportionally.

concepts.title: Thermal Energy Transfer and Equilibrium
concepts.content_html:
Thermal Energy Transfer and Equilibrium

Leave a hot cup of coffee on the counter and it cools down. Leave an ice cube in the sun and it melts. In both cases, thermal energy flows from warmer objects to cooler ones until they reach the same temperature — thermal equilibrium.

Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics

If object A is in thermal equilibrium with object C, and object B is also in thermal equilibrium with object C, then A and B are in thermal equilibrium with each other. This law justifies using thermometers: the thermometer (C) reaches equilibrium with the object, so its reading reflects the object's temperature.

Mechanisms of Heat Transfer

Thermal energy (heat) can transfer by three mechanisms:

  • Conduction: Transfer through direct molecular contact. Faster-moving molecules collide with slower ones, transferring kinetic energy. Metals are good conductors; gases and insulators are poor conductors.
  • Convection: Transfer by bulk fluid motion. Warm fluid rises (less dense), cool fluid sinks, creating convection currents. Occurs only in fluids (liquids and gases).
  • Radiation: Transfer via electromagnetic waves (infrared). Requires no medium — it works even through vacuum (e.g., sunlight reaching Earth).

Direction of Heat Flow

Heat always flows spontaneously from higher temperature to lower temperature. The amount of energy transferred depends on the temperature difference, the materials, and the contact area and time.

\[ Q = mc\Delta T \]

where \( Q \) is the heat transferred, \( m \) is mass, \( c \) is specific heat capacity, and \( \Delta T \) is the change in temperature.

Key Idea: Thermal equilibrium does not mean equal heat — it means equal temperature. A large ocean and a small cup of water can be at the same temperature, but the ocean has far more thermal energy.
AP Exam Tip: The AP exam often tests the difference between temperature and thermal energy (heat). Temperature measures average molecular kinetic energy; thermal energy is the total kinetic energy of all molecules. Two objects at the same temperature can have very different thermal energies.

problem_sets.title: Practice: Thermal Energy Transfer and Equilibrium

problems.question_html: Which method of heat transfer can occur through a vacuum?

hints.text: Conduction requires molecular contact, convection requires fluid motion. What doesn't need matter?
Radiation uses electromagnetic waves, which travel through vacuum — like sunlight reaching Earth.

solution_steps.text: Conduction requires direct contact between particles; convection requires bulk fluid movement. Both need a medium.
Radiation transfers energy via electromagnetic waves, which can travel through vacuum. This is how the Sun's energy reaches Earth.

problems.question_html: Object A at 80°C is placed in contact with Object B at 20°C. They are isolated from everything else. After a long time, what are their temperatures?

choices.text: A is at 80°C and B is at 20°C
Both are at some temperature between 20°C and 80°C
A is at 20°C and B is at 80°C

hints.text: Heat flows from hot to cold until thermal equilibrium is reached.
At thermal equilibrium, both objects are at the same temperature, somewhere between the initial temperatures.

solution_steps.text: Heat flows from A (80°C) to B (20°C) until they reach the same temperature.
The final equilibrium temperature is between 20°C and 80°C (the exact value depends on their masses and specific heats).

problems.question_html: According to the zeroth law of thermodynamics, if object A is in thermal equilibrium with object C, and object B is also in thermal equilibrium with object C, what can be said about A and B?

hints.text: The zeroth law is about transitivity of thermal equilibrium.
If A and C are at the same temperature, and B and C are at the same temperature, then A and B must be at the same temperature.

solution_steps.text: The zeroth law states that if A is in thermal equilibrium with C, and B is in thermal equilibrium with C, then A and B are in thermal equilibrium with each other.
This means A and B are at the same temperature.

problems.question_html: Warm air rising from a heater and cool air sinking near a window is an example of what type of heat transfer?

hints.text: This involves bulk movement of fluid due to density differences.
When warm fluid rises and cool fluid sinks, creating circulation, that is convection.

solution_steps.text: Warm air is less dense and rises; cool air is denser and sinks. This bulk fluid circulation is convection.

problem_sets.title: Premium: Thermal Energy Transfer and Equilibrium

problems.question_html: A 200 g aluminum block at 100°C is placed in 500 g of water at 20°C. The specific heat of aluminum is 900 J/(kg·°C) and water is 4186 J/(kg·°C). Which statement is true at thermal equilibrium?

choices.text: The final temperature is closer to 20°C than to 100°C
The aluminum loses more thermal energy than the water gains
The final temperature is closer to 100°C than to 20°C

hints.text: Compare the heat capacities: \( mc \) for each substance determines how much temperature changes per unit of energy.
Water: \( mc = 0.5 \times 4186 = 2093 \) J/°C. Aluminum: \( mc = 0.2 \times 900 = 180 \) J/°C. Water has much more thermal inertia, so the final temperature is much closer to 20°C.

solution_steps.text: Heat capacity of water: \( 0.5 \times 4186 = 2093 \) J/°C. Aluminum: \( 0.2 \times 900 = 180 \) J/°C.
Water's heat capacity is ~12× larger, so water's temperature changes very little.
Setting \( Q_{\text{lost}} = Q_{\text{gained}} \): \( 180(100 - T_f) = 2093(T_f - 20) \), solving gives \( T_f \approx 27 \)°C, much closer to 20°C.

problems.question_html: A 0.50 kg copper block (\( c = 385 \) J/(kg·°C)) at 90°C is placed in 1.0 kg of water (\( c = 4186 \) J/(kg·°C)) at 10°C. What is the equilibrium temperature in °C? Round to the nearest whole number.

hints.text: Set heat lost by copper equal to heat gained by water: \( m_c c_c (T_{c,i} - T_f) = m_w c_w (T_f - T_{w,i}) \).

concepts.title: The First Law of Thermodynamics
concepts.content_html:
The First Law of Thermodynamics

A car engine converts fuel's chemical energy into motion, but also produces waste heat. No energy is created or destroyed — it is transformed. The first law of thermodynamics is the energy conservation law applied to thermal systems.

The First Law

\[ \Delta U = Q - W \]

where:

  • \( \Delta U \) = change in internal energy of the system (J)
  • \( Q \) = heat added to the system (positive when energy flows in)
  • \( W \) = work done by the system on the surroundings (positive when the system expands)

Types of Thermodynamic Processes

  • Isobaric (constant pressure): \( W = P\Delta V \). Both \( Q \) and \( W \) are nonzero.
  • Isochoric/Isovolumetric (constant volume): \( W = 0 \) because \( \Delta V = 0 \). All heat goes to changing internal energy: \( \Delta U = Q \).
  • Isothermal (constant temperature): \( \Delta U = 0 \) for an ideal gas. Therefore \( Q = W \) — all heat input becomes work.
  • Adiabatic (no heat transfer): \( Q = 0 \). Therefore \( \Delta U = -W \). If the gas expands adiabatically, it cools; if compressed, it heats up.

Work on PV Diagrams

The work done by the gas equals the area under the curve on a \( P \)-\( V \) diagram:

\[ W = \text{area under the } P\text{-}V \text{ curve} \]

For an isobaric process: \( W = P \Delta V \). For processes where pressure changes, the area must be calculated geometrically.

Worked Example

A gas expands isobarically at \( P = 2.0 \times 10^5 \) Pa from 0.010 m\(^3\) to 0.030 m\(^3\). If 8000 J of heat is added, find \( \Delta U \).

\[ W = P\Delta V = (2.0 \times 10^5)(0.030 - 0.010) = 4000 \text{ J} \]

\[ \Delta U = Q - W = 8000 - 4000 = 4000 \text{ J} \]

Key Idea: Internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature: \( U = \frac{3}{2}nRT \) (monatomic). If \( \Delta T = 0 \), then \( \Delta U = 0 \), regardless of other changes.
AP Exam Tip: PV diagram questions are among the most common on the AP Physics 2 exam. Practice identifying process types from the shape of the curve and calculating work as the area under the curve. Remember: expansion → positive work by gas; compression → negative work by gas.

problem_sets.title: Practice: The First Law of Thermodynamics

problems.question_html: In an isochoric process, 500 J of heat is added to a gas. How much work is done by the gas?

hints.text: Isochoric means constant volume. What does that mean for work?
\( W = P\Delta V \). If \( \Delta V = 0 \), then \( W = 0 \).

solution_steps.text: In an isochoric process, the volume does not change: \( \Delta V = 0 \).
Since \( W = P\Delta V = 0 \), the gas does no work. All 500 J goes to increasing internal energy.

problems.question_html: An ideal gas undergoes an isothermal expansion. Which of the following is true?

choices.text: No heat is exchanged with the surroundings
The heat added equals the work done by the gas

hints.text: Isothermal means constant temperature. For an ideal gas, what does that mean for \( \Delta U \)?
\( \Delta U = 0 \) (ideal gas, constant \( T \)). So \( Q = W \) from the first law.

solution_steps.text: For an ideal gas, internal energy depends only on temperature. Isothermal → \( \Delta U = 0 \).
First law: \( \Delta U = Q - W \Rightarrow 0 = Q - W \Rightarrow Q = W \). The heat added equals the work done.

problems.question_html: A gas at constant pressure \( P = 1.5 \times 10^5 \) Pa expands from 0.020 m\(^3\) to 0.050 m\(^3\). How much work (in joules) does the gas do?

hints.text: For an isobaric process, \( W = P\Delta V \).

problems.question_html: An adiabatic compression is performed on a gas, doing 300 J of work on the gas. What is the change in internal energy of the gas, in joules?

hints.text: Adiabatic means \( Q = 0 \). Work is done ON the gas, so \( W \) by the gas is negative.
\( \Delta U = Q - W = 0 - (-300) = +300 \) J. Internal energy increases by 300 J.

solution_steps.text: Adiabatic: \( Q = 0 \). Work done on the gas = 300 J means \( W_{\text{by gas}} = -300 \) J.
\( \Delta U = Q - W = 0 - (-300) = +300 \) J. The gas heats up.

problem_sets.title: Premium: The First Law of Thermodynamics

problems.question_html: An ideal gas is compressed adiabatically. Which of the following must be true?

choices.text: The temperature of the gas decreases
The internal energy of the gas decreases
The temperature of the gas increases
The pressure of the gas decreases

hints.text: Adiabatic means \( Q = 0 \). If work is done ON the gas, what happens to \( \Delta U \)?
\( \Delta U = Q - W = 0 - W \). Compression → \( W < 0 \) (work BY gas is negative) → \( \Delta U > 0 \) → temperature increases.

solution_steps.text: Adiabatic: \( Q = 0 \). Compression: work is done ON the gas, so \( W_{\text{by gas}} < 0 \).
\( \Delta U = 0 - W = -W > 0 \). Internal energy increases, so temperature increases.
This is why a bicycle pump gets hot when you compress air quickly.

problems.question_html: A monatomic ideal gas undergoes a process where 600 J of heat is removed and 200 J of work is done on the gas. What is the change in temperature if the gas contains 0.50 mol? Use \( R = 8.314 \) J/(mol·K).

hints.text: First find \( \Delta U \) using the first law, then use \( \Delta U = \frac{3}{2}nR\Delta T \) for a monatomic gas.

solution_steps.text: \( Q = -600 \) J (heat removed). Work done ON gas = 200 J → \( W_{\text{by gas}} = -200 \) J.
For monatomic ideal gas: \( \Delta U = \frac{3}{2}nR\Delta T \). \( \Delta T = \frac{-400}{\frac{3}{2}(0.50)(8.314)} = \frac{-400}{6.24} \approx -64 \) K.

problems.question_html: On a PV diagram, a gas goes from state A (\( P = 3.0 \times 10^5 \) Pa, \( V = 0.010 \) m\(^3\)) to state B (\( P = 1.0 \times 10^5 \) Pa, \( V = 0.030 \) m\(^3\)) along a straight line. How much work does the gas do, in joules?

hints.text: Work is the area under the PV curve. For a straight line from A to B, use the trapezoid area formula.

solution_steps.text: Work = area under PV curve. For a straight line: \( W = \frac{1}{2}(P_A + P_B)(V_B - V_A) \).

problems.question_html: A gas undergoes a cyclic process on a PV diagram, returning to its initial state. The cycle encloses an area of 1500 J. During the cycle, 4000 J of heat is absorbed by the gas. How much heat is rejected by the gas during the cycle? Express your answer in joules.

hints.text: For a complete cycle, \( \Delta U = 0 \). The net work equals the net heat.
Net work = 1500 J = area enclosed. \( Q_{\text{net}} = Q_{\text{in}} - Q_{\text{out}} = W_{\text{net}} \). So \( Q_{\text{out}} = 4000 - 1500 = 2500 \) J.

solution_steps.text: In a cycle: \( \Delta U = 0 \), so \( Q_{\text{net}} = W_{\text{net}} \).

problems.question_html: A monatomic ideal gas undergoes the following two-step process: (1) isochoric heating from state A (\( P_A = 1.0 \times 10^5 \) Pa, \( V_A = 0.020 \) m\(^3\)) to state B (\( P_B = 3.0 \times 10^5 \) Pa), then (2) isobaric expansion from state B to state C (\( V_C = 0.060 \) m\(^3\)). Determine the total work done by the gas and the total change in internal energy. Explain each step.
problems.sample_answer: Step 1 (A→B, isochoric): W₁ = 0 (no volume change). ΔU₁ = Q₁. Step 2 (B→C, isobaric at 3.0×10⁵ Pa): W₂ = PΔV = (3.0×10⁵)(0.060 - 0.020) = 12000 J. Total work W = 0 + 12000 = 12000 J. For the total ΔU, we use ΔU = (3/2)nRΔT. Using PV = nRT: nRT_A = (1.0×10⁵)(0.020) = 2000 J, nRT_C = (3.0×10⁵)(0.060) = 18000 J. ΔU = (3/2)(nRT_C - nRT_A) = (3/2)(18000 - 2000) = 24000 J.
rubric: Correctly identifies W = 0 for isochoric step and calculates isobaric work W = PΔV = 12000 J (1 point)
Calculates total work = 12000 J with correct reasoning (1 point)
Determines total ΔU using either nRT products or first law approach, with correct final value of 24000 J (1 point)

hints.text: Break it into two steps. In Step 1, what is the work for a constant-volume process?
Step 1: \( W_1 = 0 \). Step 2: \( W_2 = P_B(V_C - V_B) \). For \( \Delta U \), use \( U = \frac{3}{2}nRT = \frac{3}{2}PV \) for a monatomic gas.

problems.correct_answer: Step 1 (A→B, isochoric): W₁ = 0 (no volume change). ΔU₁ = Q₁. Step 2 (B→C, isobaric at 3.0×10⁵ Pa): W₂ = PΔV = (3.0×10⁵)(0.060 - 0.020) = 12000 J. Total work W = 0 + 12000 = 12000 J. For the total ΔU, we use ΔU = (3/2)nRΔT. Using PV = nRT: nRT_A = (1.0×10⁵)(0.020) = 2000 J, nRT_C = (3.0×10⁵)(0.060) = 18000 J. ΔU = (3/2)(nRT_C - nRT_A) = (3/2)(18000 - 2000) = 24000 J.

concepts.title: Specific Heat and Thermal Conductivity
concepts.content_html:
Specific Heat and Thermal Conductivity

Why does a metal spoon feel colder than a wooden spoon at the same temperature? Why does water take so long to boil, yet sand at the beach gets scorching hot in minutes? The answers involve specific heat and thermal conductivity.

Specific Heat Capacity

Specific heat capacity \( c \) measures how much energy is needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 K (or 1°C):

\[ Q = mc\Delta T \]

where:

  • \( Q \) = heat transferred (J)
  • \( m \) = mass (kg)
  • \( c \) = specific heat capacity (J/(kg·K))
  • \( \Delta T = T_f - T_i \) = change in temperature (K or °C)

Water has an unusually high specific heat: \( c_{\text{water}} = 4186 \) J/(kg·K). This is why coastal climates are milder — the ocean absorbs and releases large amounts of heat with small temperature changes.

Calorimetry

When two objects at different temperatures are placed in thermal contact (and insulated from the environment), energy conservation gives:

\[ Q_{\text{lost}} = Q_{\text{gained}} \]

\[ m_1 c_1 (T_{1,i} - T_f) = m_2 c_2 (T_f - T_{2,i}) \]

Thermal Conductivity

Thermal conductivity \( k \) measures how well a material conducts heat. The rate of heat transfer through a slab is:

\[ \frac{Q}{\Delta t} = \frac{kA\Delta T}{L} \]

where:

  • \( k \) = thermal conductivity (W/(m·K))
  • \( A \) = cross-sectional area (m\(^2\))
  • \( \Delta T \) = temperature difference across the slab (K)
  • \( L \) = thickness of the slab (m)

Metals have high \( k \) (good conductors); materials like wood, plastic, and air have low \( k \) (good insulators).

Key Idea: Specific heat tells you how much energy a substance stores per degree; thermal conductivity tells you how fast it transfers that energy. A substance can have high specific heat but low conductivity (like water), or vice versa.
AP Exam Tip: In calorimetry problems, always define your system carefully. \( Q_{\text{lost}} = Q_{\text{gained}} \) only works if the system is thermally insulated (no heat escapes to the environment). Watch for sign conventions: \( Q > 0 \) means the object gains heat.

problem_sets.title: Practice: Specific Heat and Thermal Conductivity

problems.question_html: Two blocks of equal mass, one made of copper (\( c = 385 \) J/(kg·K)) and one of aluminum (\( c = 900 \) J/(kg·K)), both start at 100°C and are placed on identical ice blocks. Which melts more ice?

hints.text: The block that releases more heat to the ice will melt more. Compare \( Q = mc\Delta T \) for each.
Same mass and same \( \Delta T \), but aluminum has higher \( c \). So \( Q_{\text{Al}} > Q_{\text{Cu}} \). Aluminum releases more heat.

solution_steps.text: Both have the same mass and initial temperature, so \( Q = mc\Delta T \) depends only on \( c \).
Since \( c_{\text{Al}} = 900 > c_{\text{Cu}} = 385 \), aluminum stores more thermal energy per degree and releases more heat, melting more ice.

problems.question_html: A 0.30 kg iron block (\( c = 450 \) J/(kg·K)) at 200°C is dropped into 0.50 kg of water at 25°C. Assuming no heat loss, what is the equilibrium temperature in °C? Round to the nearest whole number.

hints.text: Set heat lost by iron = heat gained by water.

solution_steps.text: \( m_i c_i (T_{i,i} - T_f) = m_w c_w (T_f - T_{w,i}) \)

problems.question_html: How much heat (in joules) is needed to raise the temperature of 2.0 kg of water from 20°C to 80°C? Use \( c = 4186 \) J/(kg·K).

hints.text: Use \( Q = mc\Delta T \).

problems.question_html: A glass window has thermal conductivity \( k = 0.80 \) W/(m·K), area \( A = 2.0 \) m\(^2\), and thickness \( L = 0.005 \) m. If the inside surface is at 20°C and the outside at 0°C, what is the rate of heat loss through the window in watts?

hints.text: Use \( Q/\Delta t = kA\Delta T / L \).

problems.question_html: A 0.10 kg piece of unknown metal at 200°C is placed in 0.40 kg of water at 20°C. The equilibrium temperature is 23°C. What is the specific heat of the metal in J/(kg·K)? Round to the nearest whole number.

hints.text: Set \( m_m c_m (T_{m,i} - T_f) = m_w c_w (T_f - T_{w,i}) \) and solve for \( c_m \).

solution_steps.text: Heat lost by metal = heat gained by water.

problems.question_html: Two rods of the same length and cross-section are made of different materials. Rod A has \( k_A = 400 \) W/(m·K) and Rod B has \( k_B = 50 \) W/(m·K). If both have the same temperature difference across their ends, what is the ratio of heat flow rate through A to that through B?

hints.text: Rate of heat flow is proportional to \( k \) when \( A \), \( L \), and \( \Delta T \) are the same.
\( \frac{(Q/\Delta t)_A}{(Q/\Delta t)_B} = \frac{k_A}{k_B} = \frac{400}{50} = 8 \).

solution_steps.text: Since \( Q/\Delta t = kA\Delta T/L \) and all factors except \( k \) are the same:
The ratio is \( k_A/k_B = 400/50 = 8 \). Rod A conducts heat 8 times faster.

problems.question_html: A styrofoam cooler wall has \( k = 0.033 \) W/(m·K), area 0.50 m\(^2\), and thickness 0.03 m. The inside is at 5°C and outside is at 35°C. How much heat leaks into the cooler in 1 hour, in joules?

hints.text: Find the rate \( Q/\Delta t \) first, then multiply by time (in seconds).

problems.question_html: A student performs a calorimetry experiment. She places a 150 g metal sample heated to 95°C into 300 g of water at 22°C in an insulated cup. The final temperature is 25°C. Determine the specific heat of the metal, identify a possible metal, and explain one source of error that could affect the result.
problems.sample_answer: Q_water = mcΔT = (0.300)(4186)(3) = 3767.4 J. Q_metal = mcΔT: 3767.4 = (0.150)(c)(70), so c = 3767.4/(10.5) = 358.8 ≈ 359 J/(kg·K). This is close to copper (385 J/(kg·K)). One source of error: heat could be lost to the cup and surroundings, making the measured specific heat lower than the actual value since less heat appears to transfer from the metal to the water.
rubric: Correctly calculates specific heat using calorimetry equation: c ≈ 359 J/(kg·K) (1 point)
Identifies a plausible metal from the calculated value (1 point)
Explains a valid source of error and its effect on the result (1 point)

hints.text: Set heat gained by water equal to heat lost by the metal sample.
\( m_w c_w (T_f - T_{w,i}) = m_m c_m (T_{m,i} - T_f) \). Solve for \( c_m \). Then compare to known values.

solution_steps.text: Heat lost by metal: \( Q_m = (0.150)(c_m)(95 - 25) = 10.5 c_m \).
Setting equal: \( c_m = 3767/10.5 \approx 359 \) J/(kg·K). Close to copper (385 J/(kg·K)).
Error: heat loss to the cup/surroundings would mean the water gains less heat than the metal actually lost, giving a lower apparent specific heat.

problems.correct_answer: Q_water = mcΔT = (0.300)(4186)(3) = 3767.4 J. Q_metal = mcΔT: 3767.4 = (0.150)(c)(70), so c = 3767.4/(10.5) = 358.8 ≈ 359 J/(kg·K). This is close to copper (385 J/(kg·K)). One source of error: heat could be lost to the cup and surroundings, making the measured specific heat lower than the actual value since less heat appears to transfer from the metal to the water.

concepts.title: Entropy and the Second Law of Thermodynamics
concepts.content_html:
Entropy and the Second Law of Thermodynamics

You can scramble an egg, but you can't unscramble it. A hot cup of coffee cools down, but a cold cup never spontaneously heats up. These everyday observations reflect one of the deepest laws in physics: the second law of thermodynamics.

The Second Law

The total entropy of an isolated system never decreases. In any real (irreversible) process, entropy increases:

\[ \Delta S_{\text{total}} \geq 0 \]

Equality holds only for idealized reversible processes.

What Is Entropy?

Entropy \( S \) is a measure of the number of microscopic arrangements (microstates) that correspond to a macroscopic state. More disordered states have higher entropy because there are more ways to arrange the particles.

For a process at constant temperature:

\[ \Delta S = \frac{Q}{T} \]

where \( Q \) is the heat transferred and \( T \) is the absolute temperature (K).

Heat Engines and Efficiency

A heat engine converts thermal energy into work by taking heat \( Q_H \) from a hot reservoir, doing work \( W \), and rejecting heat \( Q_C \) to a cold reservoir:

\[ W = Q_H - Q_C \]

Efficiency:

\[ e = \frac{W}{Q_H} = 1 - \frac{Q_C}{Q_H} \]

The second law guarantees that \( e < 1 \) — no heat engine can convert all heat into work.

Carnot Efficiency

The maximum possible efficiency for a heat engine operating between temperatures \( T_H \) and \( T_C \):

\[ e_{\text{Carnot}} = 1 - \frac{T_C}{T_H} \]

where temperatures must be in Kelvin. No real engine can exceed this efficiency.

Key Idea: Entropy is not about "mess" in the everyday sense — it's about probability. A system evolves toward the macrostate with the most microstates because that's overwhelmingly the most likely outcome.
AP Exam Tip: The second law does NOT forbid local decreases in entropy (like a refrigerator making ice). It says the total entropy of the universe increases. When a refrigerator cools food, it dumps even more heat into the room, increasing total entropy. Questions often test this distinction.

problem_sets.title: Practice: Entropy and the Second Law

problems.question_html: Which of the following statements is consistent with the second law of thermodynamics?

choices.text: Heat can flow spontaneously from a cold object to a hot object
A heat engine can be 100% efficient
The entropy of the universe tends to increase
Energy can be created in thermal processes

hints.text: The second law is about the direction of natural processes and entropy.
The second law states that the total entropy of an isolated system (or the universe) never decreases.

solution_steps.text: The second law states that the entropy of the universe tends to increase in all natural processes.
Heat flows spontaneously from hot to cold (not the reverse). No engine is 100% efficient. Energy is conserved (first law), not created.

problems.question_html: A heat engine absorbs 1000 J from a hot reservoir and exhausts 600 J to a cold reservoir. What is the efficiency of the engine?

hints.text: Efficiency = work output / heat input. First find the work.

problems.question_html: 500 J of heat is added to a system at a constant temperature of 250 K. What is the change in entropy of the system, in J/K?

hints.text: Use \( \Delta S = Q/T \).

problems.question_html: What is the maximum theoretical efficiency (in percent) of a heat engine operating between a hot reservoir at 600 K and a cold reservoir at 300 K?

hints.text: Use the Carnot efficiency formula.

problem_sets.title: Premium: Entropy and the Second Law

problems.question_html: A heat engine operates between a hot reservoir at 800 K and a cold reservoir at 200 K. If the engine absorbs 2000 J per cycle, what is the maximum work it can produce per cycle?

hints.text: Find the Carnot efficiency first, then multiply by \( Q_H \).

problems.question_html: 1000 J of heat flows from a reservoir at 500 K to a reservoir at 250 K. What is the total entropy change of the two-reservoir system, in J/K?

hints.text: Calculate \( \Delta S \) for each reservoir separately, then add.

solution_steps.text: Hot reservoir loses heat: \( \Delta S_H = -Q/T_H = -1000/500 = -2 \) J/K.
Cold reservoir gains heat: \( \Delta S_C = +Q/T_C = +1000/250 = +4 \) J/K.
Total: \( \Delta S_{\text{total}} = -2 + 4 = +2 \) J/K > 0. Entropy increases, as expected for an irreversible process.

problems.question_html: A power plant operates at 35% efficiency and produces 500 MW of electrical power. How much heat (in MW) must be rejected to the cold reservoir per second?

hints.text: Efficiency \( e = W/Q_H \). First find \( Q_H \), then \( Q_C = Q_H - W \).

problems.question_html: A Carnot engine operates between 700 K and 350 K and does 500 J of work per cycle. Determine (a) the efficiency, (b) the heat absorbed from the hot reservoir, and (c) the heat rejected to the cold reservoir. Show your reasoning for each part.
rubric: Correctly calculates Carnot efficiency: e = 50% (1 point)
Correctly determines Q_H = 1000 J from e = W/Q_H (1 point)
Correctly determines Q_C = 500 J from energy conservation (1 point)

hints.text: Start with the Carnot efficiency formula, then use \( e = W/Q_H \) and \( Q_H = Q_C + W \).

concepts.title: Electric Charge and Electric Force
concepts.content_html:
Electric Charge and Electric Force

Rub a balloon on your hair and it sticks to the wall. Shuffle across a carpet and touch a doorknob — zap! These everyday phenomena arise from electric charge, one of the fundamental properties of matter.

Electric Charge

There are two types of charge: positive and negative. Protons carry positive charge; electrons carry negative charge. The elementary charge is:

\[ e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C} \]

Charge is quantized: it always comes in integer multiples of \( e \). Charge is also conserved: the total charge of an isolated system never changes.

Coulomb's Law

The electric force between two point charges is:

\[ F = k \frac{|q_1||q_2|}{r^2} \]

where:

  • \( F \) = magnitude of the electric force (N)
  • \( k = 8.99 \times 10^9 \) N·m²/C² = Coulomb's constant
  • \( q_1, q_2 \) = the two charges (C)
  • \( r \) = distance between the charges (m)

Like charges repel; opposite charges attract. The force is along the line connecting the charges.

Superposition

When multiple charges are present, the net force on any charge is the vector sum of the individual Coulomb forces from each other charge.

Key Idea: Coulomb's law has the same mathematical form as Newton's law of gravitation (\( F \propto 1/r^2 \)), but electric forces can be attractive or repulsive, while gravity is always attractive. Electric forces are also enormously stronger than gravitational forces at the atomic scale.
AP Exam Tip: When using Coulomb's law, \( r \) is the distance between the charges, not the radius of anything. If the distance doubles, the force decreases by a factor of 4. The exam frequently tests this inverse-square relationship.

problem_sets.title: Practice: Electric Charge and Electric Force

problems.question_html: Two point charges of \( +3 \) μC and \( -3 \) μC are separated by 0.10 m. Is the force between them attractive or repulsive, and what is its magnitude? (Use \( k = 9.0 \times 10^9 \) N·m²/C².)

hints.text: Opposite charges attract. Use Coulomb's law for magnitude.

solution_steps.text: The charges are opposite, so the force is attractive.

problems.question_html: If the distance between two point charges is tripled, by what factor does the electric force between them change?

choices.text: It decreases by a factor of 3
It decreases by a factor of 9
It increases by a factor of 3
It increases by a factor of 9

hints.text: Coulomb's law is an inverse-square law: \( F \propto 1/r^2 \).
If \( r \to 3r \), then \( F \to F/(3^2) = F/9 \).

solution_steps.text: \( F \propto 1/r^2 \). Tripling \( r \) gives \( F' = F/3^2 = F/9 \).
The force decreases by a factor of 9.

problems.question_html: Two identical positive charges of 4.0 μC are separated by 0.20 m. What is the magnitude of the electric force between them, in newtons? Use \( k = 9.0 \times 10^9 \) N·m²/C².

hints.text: Use \( F = kq^2/r^2 \) since the charges are identical.

problems.question_html: An object has a net charge of \( -4.8 \times 10^{-19} \) C. How many excess electrons does it have?

hints.text: Each electron carries a charge of \( -1.6 \times 10^{-19} \) C.
Number of excess electrons = \( |q|/e = (4.8 \times 10^{-19})/(1.6 \times 10^{-19}) = 3 \).

problem_sets.title: Premium: Electric Charge and Electric Force

problems.question_html: Three charges are placed along the x-axis: \( q_1 = +2 \) μC at \( x = 0 \), \( q_2 = -4 \) μC at \( x = 0.30 \) m, and \( q_3 = +2 \) μC at \( x = 0.60 \) m. What is the direction of the net force on \( q_2 \)?

choices.text: Cannot be determined without calculating magnitudes

hints.text: Consider the force on \( q_2 \) from \( q_1 \) and from \( q_3 \) separately. What are the directions?
\( q_1 \) attracts \( q_2 \) to the left. \( q_3 \) attracts \( q_2 \) to the right. Since \( q_1 = q_3 \) and both are equidistant from \( q_2 \), the forces cancel.

solution_steps.text: Force from \( q_1 \): attractive (\( q_2 \) is negative, \( q_1 \) is positive) → pulls \( q_2 \) to the left.
Force from \( q_3 \): attractive → pulls \( q_2 \) to the right.
Since \( |q_1| = |q_3| = 2 \) μC and both are 0.30 m from \( q_2 \), the forces have equal magnitude and opposite direction. Net force = 0.

problems.question_html: Two charges \( q_1 = +5.0 \) μC and \( q_2 = +5.0 \) μC are 0.40 m apart. What is the magnitude of the force on each charge, in newtons? Round to two decimal places.

hints.text: Use Coulomb's law. By Newton's third law, the force on each is the same magnitude.

concepts.title: Conservation of Electric Charge and the Process of Charging
concepts.content_html:
Conservation of Electric Charge and the Process of Charging

When you rub a balloon on your hair, the balloon doesn't create charge — it steals electrons from your hair. Charge is never created or destroyed; it is only transferred.

Conservation of Charge

The total electric charge in an isolated system is constant. Charge can be transferred between objects, but the total amount remains the same.

Methods of Charging

  • Friction (Triboelectric): Rubbing two different materials transfers electrons from one to the other. The material that loses electrons becomes positive; the one that gains becomes negative.
  • Conduction (Contact): Touching a charged object to a neutral conductor transfers charge. The charges redistribute until both objects are at the same potential. Both end up with the same sign of charge.
  • Induction: Bringing a charged object near (but not touching) a conductor causes charge separation. If the conductor is grounded during this process, charge flows to/from ground, leaving the conductor with a net charge opposite to the inducing charge.

Conductors vs. Insulators

Conductors (metals) have free electrons that move easily. Charge distributes on the surface. Insulators (rubber, glass) hold charge in place — charge stays where it is placed.

In a conductor at equilibrium, the electric field inside is zero and all excess charge resides on the surface.

Key Idea: Charging by induction allows you to charge an object without ever touching it to the charged source. The key step is grounding: connecting the conductor to Earth so that charge can flow in or out.
AP Exam Tip: When two identical conducting spheres touch, they share their total charge equally. If one has +6 μC and the other −2 μC, after contact each has \( (+6 + (−2))/2 = +2 \) μC. The exam tests this frequently.

problem_sets.title: Practice: Conservation of Charge and Charging

problems.question_html: Two identical conducting spheres carry charges of \( +8 \) μC and \( -2 \) μC. They are brought into contact and then separated. What is the charge on each sphere after separation?

hints.text: Identical spheres share charge equally when in contact.
Total charge = \( +8 + (-2) = +6 \) μC. Divided equally: \( +3 \) μC each.

solution_steps.text: Identical spheres share equally: \( +6/2 = +3 \) μC on each.

problems.question_html: A negatively charged rod is brought near a neutral metal sphere without touching it. What happens to the charge distribution on the sphere?

choices.text: Positive charge moves to the near side; negative charge to the far side
Negative charge moves to the near side; positive to the far side
Nothing happens because the rod doesn't touch the sphere

hints.text: Free electrons in the conductor are repelled or attracted by the rod's charge.
The negative rod repels electrons in the sphere to the far side, leaving the near side positively charged (charge separation by induction).

solution_steps.text: The negative rod repels free electrons in the metal sphere, pushing them to the far side.
The near side becomes positive (deficit of electrons) and the far side becomes negative (excess electrons). The sphere is still neutral overall — charges have only separated.

problems.question_html: When a glass rod is rubbed with silk, the rod becomes positively charged. What happened at the atomic level?

hints.text: Charge is conserved. If the rod becomes positive, it must have lost something.
Electrons transferred from the glass rod to the silk. The rod lost electrons and became positive.

solution_steps.text: Electrons were transferred from the glass rod to the silk. The rod lost electrons, giving it a net positive charge. The silk gained those electrons, becoming negatively charged.

problems.question_html: In charging by induction, the object being charged ends up with what sign of charge relative to the inducing charge?

hints.text: Think about what happens when you ground the conductor while the charged object is nearby.
Grounding allows charge to flow, leaving the conductor with a charge opposite to the inducing charge.

solution_steps.text: In charging by induction (with grounding), the induced object acquires a charge opposite to the inducing charge.
A positive rod induces a negative charge; a negative rod induces a positive charge.

problem_sets.title: Premium: Conservation of Charge and Charging

problems.question_html: Sphere A has charge \( +12 \) μC and sphere B has charge \( -4 \) μC. They touch, separate, then sphere B touches neutral sphere C (identical to A and B). What is the final charge on sphere C?

hints.text: First find the charge on A and B after they touch (total shared equally). Then B touches C.
A+B total: \( 12 + (-4) = 8 \) μC → 4 μC each. Then B (+4 μC) touches C (0): \( (4+0)/2 = +2 \) μC each.

solution_steps.text: Step 1: A and B touch. Total = \( 12 + (-4) = 8 \) μC. Each gets \( 8/2 = +4 \) μC.
Step 2: B (+4 μC) touches C (0 μC). Total = 4 μC. Each gets \( 4/2 = +2 \) μC.

problems.question_html: A neutral metal sphere is placed on an insulating stand. A positively charged rod is brought near (but not touching) the left side. While the rod is still nearby, the sphere is grounded momentarily, then the ground connection is removed, then the rod is removed. What is the final charge on the sphere?

hints.text: While the positive rod is near, what happens to electrons in the sphere? What does grounding do?

The positive rod attracts electrons to the near side. Grounding allows additional electrons to flow onto the sphere from the ground. When ground is removed and rod is removed, the sphere retains the extra electrons → negative.

solution_steps.text: The positive rod attracts electrons to the near side and repels positive charge to the far side.
Grounding allows electrons from the ground to flow onto the sphere (attracted by the positive rod).
Ground removed → extra electrons are trapped. Rod removed → electrons redistribute. The sphere is now negatively charged.

concepts.title: Electric Fields
concepts.content_html:
Electric Fields

How does one charge "know" another is there? The answer is the electric field — a region of space where electric forces act. Rather than thinking of charges exerting forces on each other across empty space, we say each charge creates a field, and other charges interact with that field.

Electric Field Definition

The electric field at a point is the force per unit positive test charge:

\[ \vec{E} = \frac{\vec{F}}{q_0} \]

where \( q_0 \) is a small positive test charge. Units: N/C or equivalently V/m.

Field Due to a Point Charge

\[ E = k\frac{|Q|}{r^2} \]

The field points radially outward from a positive charge and radially inward toward a negative charge.

Electric Field Lines

  • Field lines begin on positive charges and end on negative charges.
  • The density of lines indicates field strength — closer lines mean stronger field.
  • Lines never cross.
  • At any point, the field direction is tangent to the field line.

Superposition of Fields

The total electric field at a point is the vector sum of the fields from all individual charges:

\[ \vec{E}_{\text{net}} = \vec{E}_1 + \vec{E}_2 + \cdots \]

Uniform Electric Field

Between two large parallel plates with equal and opposite charge, the field is approximately uniform (constant magnitude and direction):

\[ E = \frac{V}{d} \]

where \( V \) is the voltage across the plates and \( d \) is their separation.

Key Idea: The electric field is a vector field — it has both magnitude and direction at every point. A positive charge experiences a force in the direction of \( \vec{E} \); a negative charge experiences a force opposite to \( \vec{E} \).
AP Exam Tip: Don't confuse the source charge \( Q \) (which creates the field) with the test charge \( q_0 \) (which experiences the field). The field \( E = kQ/r^2 \) depends only on the source charge and the distance — not on the test charge.

problems.question_html: A charge of \( +2.0 \) μC creates an electric field. At a distance of 0.50 m from the charge, what is the magnitude of the electric field? (Use \( k = 9.0 \times 10^9 \) N·m²/C².)

hints.text: Use \( E = kQ/r^2 \).

solution_steps.text: \( = 1.8 \times 10^4/0.25 = 7.2 \times 10^4 \) N/C, directed radially outward from the positive charge.

problems.question_html: A positive test charge is placed in an electric field and experiences a force pointing to the right. In what direction does the electric field point at that location?

hints.text: The electric field direction is defined as the direction a positive test charge would be pushed.
Since a positive charge is pushed to the right, the field points to the right.

solution_steps.text: By definition, \( \vec{E} = \vec{F}/q_0 \). For a positive \( q_0 \), \( \vec{E} \) is in the same direction as \( \vec{F} \).
The field points to the right.

problems.question_html: The electric field at a point is 500 N/C. What force (in newtons) acts on a \( -3.0 \) μC charge placed at that point? Give the magnitude.

hints.text: Use \( F = |q|E \).

solution_steps.text: The force direction is opposite to \( \vec{E} \) because the charge is negative.

problems.question_html: At what distance (in meters) from a \( +8.0 \) μC point charge is the electric field equal to \( 2.0 \times 10^6 \) N/C? Round to two decimal places.

hints.text: Rearrange \( E = kQ/r^2 \) to solve for \( r \).

problems.question_html: Two charges \( q_1 = +4.0 \) μC at the origin and \( q_2 = -4.0 \) μC at \( x = 0.40 \) m. What is the electric field at the midpoint (\( x = 0.20 \) m)?

hints.text: Find E from each charge at the midpoint, then add as vectors. What direction does each field point?

At midpoint: E from \( q_1 \) (positive) points to the right. E from \( q_2 \) (negative) also points to the right (toward the negative charge). Both add. \( E = 2 \times kQ/r^2 = 2(9 \times 10^9)(4 \times 10^{-6})/(0.20)^2 = 1.8 \times 10^6 \) N/C.

solution_steps.text: At the midpoint, each charge is 0.20 m away. \( E_1 = kq_1/r^2 = (9 \times 10^9)(4 \times 10^{-6})/(0.04) = 9 \times 10^5 \) N/C.
\( E_1 \) points to the right (away from positive \( q_1 \)). \( E_2 \) also points to the right (toward negative \( q_2 \)). Same direction.

problems.question_html: Two large parallel plates are separated by 0.02 m and have a potential difference of 500 V across them. What is the magnitude of the uniform electric field between the plates, in V/m?

hints.text: For parallel plates, \( E = V/d \).

problems.question_html: A \( +6.0 \) μC charge is at the origin. At what distance from the charge (in meters) is the electric field strength \( 5400 \) N/C?

hints.text: Rearrange \( E = kQ/r^2 \) to find \( r \).
\( r = \sqrt{kQ/E} = \sqrt{(9 \times 10^9)(6 \times 10^{-6})/5400} = \sqrt{10} \approx 3.16 \) m.

problems.question_html: A proton (\( m = 1.67 \times 10^{-27} \) kg, \( q = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \) C) is placed in a uniform electric field of \( E = 2.0 \times 10^4 \) N/C. Determine the acceleration of the proton and explain why the electron would have a much larger acceleration in the same field.
problems.sample_answer: F = qE = (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹)(2.0 × 10⁴) = 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ N. a = F/m = 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ / 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ = 1.9 × 10¹² m/s². An electron has the same charge magnitude but much less mass (9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg), so a = F/m would be about 1836 times larger.
rubric: Correctly calculates force F = qE = 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ N (1 point)
Correctly calculates acceleration a = F/m ≈ 1.9 × 10¹² m/s² (1 point)
Explains that the electron's smaller mass leads to greater acceleration for the same force (1 point)

hints.text: Use \( F = qE \), then \( a = F/m \).
The electron has the same charge magnitude but mass 1836× smaller than the proton.

solution_steps.text: An electron has the same \( |q| \) but \( m_e = 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \) kg (1836× less than proton). Same force, much less mass → \( a_e \approx 1836 \times a_p \approx 3.5 \times 10^{15} \) m/s².

problems.correct_answer: F = qE = (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹)(2.0 × 10⁴) = 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ N. a = F/m = 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ / 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ = 1.9 × 10¹² m/s². An electron has the same charge magnitude but much less mass (9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg), so a = F/m would be about 1836 times larger.

concepts.title: Electric Potential Energy
concepts.content_html:
Electric Potential Energy

Just as a ball on a hilltop has gravitational potential energy, a charged particle in an electric field has electric potential energy. When a positive charge moves in the direction of the electric field, it "falls downhill" — losing potential energy and gaining kinetic energy.

Potential Energy of Point Charges

The electric potential energy of two point charges separated by distance \( r \):

\[ U = k \frac{q_1 q_2}{r} \]

Note: unlike the force formula, this is not squared in the denominator. Also, include the signs of the charges:

  • Like charges (both + or both −): \( U > 0 \) — energy must be added to bring them together.
  • Unlike charges (one +, one −): \( U < 0 \) — they are bound; energy must be added to separate them.

Work and Potential Energy

The work done by the electric force equals the negative change in potential energy:

\[ W_{\text{electric}} = -\Delta U = -(U_f - U_i) \]

If a positive charge moves from high potential energy to low potential energy, the electric force does positive work (like gravity pulling a ball downhill).

Conservation of Energy

In the absence of other forces:

\[ K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f \]

This lets us find speeds of charged particles after being released from rest in an electric field.

Key Idea: Electric potential energy depends on the configuration of charges, not on a single charge. It takes two (or more) charges to have electric potential energy, just as it takes a mass and a gravitational field to have gravitational PE.
AP Exam Tip: Pay attention to signs! The formula \( U = kq_1q_2/r \) automatically gives the correct sign. Don't use absolute values here (unlike in Coulomb's force law). A negative \( U \) means the charges are bound together.

problems.question_html: Two protons are separated by \( 1.0 \times 10^{-10} \) m. What is the sign of their electric potential energy?

hints.text: Both protons are positive. What does \( U = kq_1q_2/r \) give when both charges are positive?
\( U = k(+)(+)/r > 0 \). Like charges have positive potential energy.

solution_steps.text: Both charges are positive, so \( q_1 q_2 > 0 \) and \( U = kq_1q_2/r > 0 \).
Positive PE means energy was required to bring them this close (they repel).

problems.question_html: What is the electric potential energy (in joules) of a system of two charges, \( q_1 = +3.0 \) μC and \( q_2 = -6.0 \) μC, separated by 0.30 m?

hints.text: Use \( U = kq_1q_2/r \) with signs.

solution_steps.text: \( = (9 \times 10^9)(-18 \times 10^{-12})/0.30 = -0.54 \) J. Negative because unlike charges are bound.

problems.question_html: A \( +2.0 \) μC charge is released from rest at a point where the electric potential energy is 0.010 J. It moves to a point where \( U = 0.002 \) J. What is its kinetic energy at the second point, in joules?

hints.text: Use conservation of energy: \( K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f \). The charge starts from rest.

solution_steps.text: Conservation of energy: \( K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f \).

problems.question_html: Two charges, \( q_1 = +4.0 \) μC and \( q_2 = +4.0 \) μC, are initially 0.10 m apart. How much work must an external agent do to bring them to 0.05 m apart, in joules? Round to two decimal places.

hints.text: Work by external agent = \( \Delta U = U_f - U_i \).

problems.question_html: An electron (\( m = 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \) kg) is released from rest in a uniform electric field and gains \( 4.8 \times 10^{-18} \) J of kinetic energy. Through what potential energy change (in eV) did it pass?

hints.text: The kinetic energy gained equals the potential energy lost. Convert J to eV.

solution_steps.text: By energy conservation: \( \Delta K = -\Delta U \). The electron gained \( 4.8 \times 10^{-18} \) J, so it lost \( 4.8 \times 10^{-18} \) J of PE.

problems.question_html: Three charges are at the corners of an equilateral triangle with side 0.20 m: \( q_1 = +1.0 \) μC, \( q_2 = +1.0 \) μC, \( q_3 = -1.0 \) μC. What is the total electric potential energy of the system, in joules? Round to three decimal places.

hints.text: Total PE = sum of all pairwise potential energies: \( U_{12} + U_{13} + U_{23} \).

problems.question_html: A proton (\( q = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \) C, \( m = 1.67 \times 10^{-27} \) kg) is released from rest at 0.50 m from a fixed \( +2.0 \) nC charge. What is the proton's speed (in m/s) when it is 5.0 m away? Round to the nearest thousand.

hints.text: Use conservation of energy: \( K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f \).
\( 0 + kqQ/r_i = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 + kqQ/r_f \). Solve for \( v \).

problems.question_html: Two point charges \( q_1 = +3.0 \) μC and \( q_2 = -5.0 \) μC are separated by 0.40 m. Determine the total electric potential energy of the system and explain what the sign of the result means physically.
problems.sample_answer: U = kq₁q₂/r = (9.0 × 10⁹)(3.0 × 10⁻⁶)(−5.0 × 10⁻⁶)/0.40 = −0.3375 J ≈ −0.34 J. The negative sign means the charges are bound to each other — you would need to do +0.34 J of work to separate them to infinity. This makes sense because opposite charges attract.
rubric: Correctly applies U = kq₁q₂/r with proper signs (1 point)
Arrives at correct numerical answer: U ≈ −0.34 J (1 point)
Explains the physical meaning of the negative sign (bound system, work needed to separate) (1 point)

hints.text: Use \( U = kq_1q_2/r \) — include the signs of the charges.
Negative PE means the configuration is bound — energy must be added to pull the charges apart.

solution_steps.text: Negative PE means the charges attract and are "bound" — 0.34 J of work would be needed to separate them to infinity.

problems.correct_answer: U = kq₁q₂/r = (9.0 × 10⁹)(3.0 × 10⁻⁶)(−5.0 × 10⁻⁶)/0.40 = −0.3375 J ≈ −0.34 J. The negative sign means the charges are bound to each other — you would need to do +0.34 J of work to separate them to infinity. This makes sense because opposite charges attract.

concepts.title: Electric Potential
concepts.content_html:
Electric Potential

A 9-volt battery maintains a potential difference of 9 V between its terminals. This electric potential — commonly called voltage — is one of the most practical concepts in physics and engineering.

Definition

Electric potential at a point is the electric potential energy per unit charge:

\[ V = \frac{U}{q} \]

Units: volts (V) = joules per coulomb (J/C).

Potential Due to a Point Charge

\[ V = k\frac{q}{r} \]

Note: unlike the field, potential is a scalar — no direction to worry about. Positive charges create positive potential; negative charges create negative potential.

Potential Difference

The potential difference (voltage) between two points determines how much work is done moving a charge:

\[ \Delta V = V_B - V_A = -\frac{W_{\text{electric}}}{q} \]

A positive charge naturally moves from high potential to low potential (like a ball rolling downhill).

Relationship Between Field and Potential

For a uniform electric field:

\[ \Delta V = -Ed \]

where \( d \) is the displacement along the field direction. The electric field points from high to low potential.

Equipotential Surfaces

An equipotential surface connects points of equal potential. Key properties:

  • No work is done moving a charge along an equipotential surface.
  • Equipotential surfaces are always perpendicular to electric field lines.
  • The surface of a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium is an equipotential surface.
Key Idea: Electric potential is a scalar — just add the potentials from individual charges directly (no vector components needed). This makes potential calculations much simpler than field calculations.
AP Exam Tip: The sign of \( V = kq/r \) depends on the sign of the source charge \( q \). Don't take absolute values here. Also, potential is defined relative to infinity (where \( V = 0 \)), not relative to ground.

problems.question_html: What is the electric potential at a distance of 0.30 m from a \( +6.0 \) μC point charge? (Use \( k = 9.0 \times 10^9 \) N·m²/C².)

hints.text: Use \( V = kq/r \).

problems.question_html: A charge of \( +2.0 \) μC moves through a potential difference of \( \Delta V = -500 \) V. How much work is done by the electric force, in joules?

hints.text: \( W = -q\Delta V \).

solution_steps.text: Positive work means the charge moved from high to low potential — the field did the pushing.

problems.question_html: Two large parallel plates have a potential difference of 200 V and are separated by 0.04 m. What is the electric field between them, in V/m?

hints.text: For parallel plates, \( E = V/d \).

problems.question_html: A \( -3.0 \) μC charge is at \( x = 0 \) and a \( +3.0 \) μC charge is at \( x = 0.60 \) m. What is the electric potential at the midpoint \( x = 0.30 \) m, in volts?

hints.text: Potential is a scalar — just add \( V_1 + V_2 \) (no vectors needed).

problems.question_html: An electron moves from a point where \( V = 100 \) V to a point where \( V = 0 \) V. What is the change in kinetic energy of the electron, in eV?

hints.text: \( \Delta K = -q\Delta V \). Remember the electron has charge \( q = -e \).
\( \Delta K = -(-e)(0 - 100) = -e \times 100 = -100 \) eV. The electron loses kinetic energy (slows down) moving from low to high potential for a negative charge.

solution_steps.text: In eV: \( -1.6 \times 10^{-17} / 1.6 \times 10^{-19} = -100 \) eV. The electron slows down because it's moving against the electric force.

problems.question_html: At what point along the x-axis (other than infinity) is the electric potential zero due to charges \( q_1 = +4.0 \) μC at the origin and \( q_2 = -2.0 \) μC at \( x = 0.60 \) m?

hints.text: Set \( V_1 + V_2 = 0 \): \( kq_1/(x) + kq_2/(0.60 - x) = 0 \). The point must be between the charges.

problems.question_html: A uniform electric field of 3000 V/m points from left to right. What is the potential difference between two points separated by 0.15 m along the field direction? (Give \( V_B - V_A \) where A is on the left and B is on the right.)

hints.text: \( \Delta V = -Ed \) when moving along the field direction.
\( V_B - V_A = -(3000)(0.15) = -450 \) V. Potential decreases in the field direction.

solution_steps.text: Electric potential decreases in the direction of the electric field.

problems.question_html: A \( +5.0 \) μC charge is at the origin. (a) Calculate the electric potential at \( r = 0.20 \) m and at \( r = 0.50 \) m. (b) Determine the work done by the electric force in moving a \( +2.0 \) μC charge from \( r = 0.20 \) m to \( r = 0.50 \) m.
rubric: Correctly calculates V at both distances (1 point)
Uses W = -qΔV or energy conservation correctly (1 point)
Correct final answer: W = +0.27 J with correct sign and units (1 point)

hints.text: Part (a): \( V = kq/r \). Part (b): \( W = -q\Delta V \).
The charge moves from higher V to lower V (away from the positive source), so the electric force does positive work.

concepts.title: Capacitors
concepts.content_html:
Capacitors

Every time you use a camera flash, a capacitor dumps its stored energy in a fraction of a second. Capacitors are devices that store electric charge and energy, found in nearly every electronic device.

What Is a Capacitor?

A capacitor consists of two conductors (plates) separated by an insulating gap (or dielectric). When connected to a battery, charge flows onto the plates: \( +Q \) on one, \( -Q \) on the other.

Capacitance

\[ C = \frac{Q}{V} \]

where:

  • \( C \) = capacitance (farads, F)
  • \( Q \) = charge on one plate (C)
  • \( V \) = voltage across the plates (V)

1 farad is very large — typical capacitors are in μF, nF, or pF.

Parallel-Plate Capacitor

For two parallel plates of area \( A \) separated by distance \( d \):

\[ C = \frac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d} \]

where \( \varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \) F/m is the permittivity of free space. A dielectric material between the plates increases capacitance by a factor \( \kappa \) (the dielectric constant):

\[ C = \frac{\kappa \varepsilon_0 A}{d} \]

Energy Stored

The energy stored in a capacitor:

\[ U = \frac{1}{2}CV^2 = \frac{Q^2}{2C} = \frac{1}{2}QV \]

Combinations

  • Parallel: \( C_{\text{eq}} = C_1 + C_2 + \cdots \) (same voltage, charges add)
  • Series: \( \frac{1}{C_{\text{eq}}} = \frac{1}{C_1} + \frac{1}{C_2} + \cdots \) (same charge, voltages add)
Key Idea: Capacitors in parallel add directly (like resistors in series), while capacitors in series add reciprocally (like resistors in parallel). This is opposite to the rule for resistors!
AP Exam Tip: When a dielectric is inserted into a capacitor that is disconnected from the battery, \( Q \) stays the same but \( C \) increases, so \( V = Q/C \) decreases. If the capacitor remains connected to the battery, \( V \) stays the same but \( Q = CV \) increases. The exam tests both scenarios.

problems.question_html: A 10 μF capacitor is charged to 100 V. What charge is stored on each plate?

hints.text: Use \( Q = CV \).

problems.question_html: A parallel-plate capacitor has plate area \( A = 0.010 \) m² and separation \( d = 0.002 \) m. What is its capacitance? (Use \( \varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \) F/m.)

hints.text: Use \( C = \varepsilon_0 A / d \).

problems.question_html: How much energy is stored in a 20 μF capacitor charged to 50 V? Give your answer in joules.

hints.text: Use \( U = \frac{1}{2}CV^2 \).

problems.question_html: Two capacitors, 6 μF and 3 μF, are connected in series. What is their equivalent capacitance in μF?

hints.text: For series: \( 1/C_{\text{eq}} = 1/C_1 + 1/C_2 \).

solution_steps.text: \( C_{\text{eq}} = 2 \) μF. Series always gives less than the smallest individual capacitor.

problems.question_html: Three capacitors of 4 μF, 6 μF, and 12 μF are connected in parallel. What is the equivalent capacitance in μF?

hints.text: For parallel capacitors: \( C_{\text{eq}} = C_1 + C_2 + C_3 \).

problems.question_html: A 5 μF capacitor is charged to 200 V, then disconnected from the battery. A dielectric with \( \kappa = 4 \) is inserted between the plates. What is the new voltage across the capacitor?

hints.text: Disconnected from battery → Q is constant. Dielectric increases C by factor κ. What happens to V = Q/C?

solution_steps.text: Initial charge: \( Q = CV = (5 \times 10^{-6})(200) = 1.0 \times 10^{-3} \) C. Disconnected → Q constant.

problems.question_html: A 100 μF capacitor stores 0.50 J of energy. What is the voltage across it, in volts?

hints.text: Use \( U = \frac{1}{2}CV^2 \) and solve for \( V \).

problems.question_html: A parallel-plate capacitor with capacitance \( C = 50 \) pF is connected to a 12 V battery. (a) How much charge is stored? (b) How much energy is stored? (c) If the plate separation is doubled while the battery remains connected, what happens to the charge and energy? Explain using the relevant equations.
problems.sample_answer: (a) Q = CV = (50 × 10⁻¹²)(12) = 600 × 10⁻¹² C = 600 pC. (b) U = ½CV² = ½(50 × 10⁻¹²)(144) = 3.6 × 10⁻⁹ J = 3.6 nJ. (c) Doubling d halves C (since C = ε₀A/d). Battery connected → V stays at 12 V. New Q = C'V = (25 pF)(12 V) = 300 pC (halved). New U = ½C'V² = ½(25 × 10⁻¹²)(144) = 1.8 nJ (halved). Charge and energy both decrease by half.
rubric: Correctly calculates Q = 600 pC and U = 3.6 nJ (1 point)
Correctly identifies that C halves when d doubles (C = ε₀A/d) (1 point)
Correctly explains that with battery connected V is constant, so Q and U both halve (1 point)

hints.text: \( Q = CV \), \( U = \frac{1}{2}CV^2 \), and \( C = \varepsilon_0 A/d \).
When the battery stays connected, voltage is fixed. Doubling \( d \) halves \( C \), so both \( Q \) and \( U \) halve.

solution_steps.text: (c) Doubling \( d \): \( C' = C/2 = 25 \) pF. Battery connected → \( V = 12 \) V. \( Q' = 300 \) pC, \( U' = 1.8 \) nJ. Both halved.

problems.correct_answer: (a) Q = CV = (50 × 10⁻¹²)(12) = 600 × 10⁻¹² C = 600 pC. (b) U = ½CV² = ½(50 × 10⁻¹²)(144) = 3.6 × 10⁻⁹ J = 3.6 nJ. (c) Doubling d halves C (since C = ε₀A/d). Battery connected → V stays at 12 V. New Q = C'V = (25 pF)(12 V) = 300 pC (halved). New U = ½C'V² = ½(25 × 10⁻¹²)(144) = 1.8 nJ (halved). Charge and energy both decrease by half.

concepts.title: Conservation of Electric Energy
concepts.content_html:
Conservation of Electric Energy

When lightning strikes, enormous amounts of electric potential energy convert to light, heat, and sound in an instant. The principle of conservation of energy applies to all electrical systems — the total energy (kinetic + electric potential) of charged particles is conserved in the absence of non-conservative forces.

Energy Conservation for Charged Particles

For a charged particle moving in an electric field (no friction or other non-conservative forces):

\[ K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f \]

\[ \frac{1}{2}mv_i^2 + qV_i = \frac{1}{2}mv_f^2 + qV_f \]

This is the work-energy theorem applied to electric systems.

The Electron-Volt (eV)

A convenient energy unit for atomic-scale problems:

\[ 1 \text{ eV} = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J} \]

One eV is the kinetic energy gained by an electron accelerated through a potential difference of 1 V.

Energy in Capacitor Circuits

The energy stored in a capacitor is \( U = \frac{1}{2}CV^2 \). When capacitors are connected or disconnected, total charge is conserved, but energy may be lost (to heat in connecting wires or radiation).

Worked Example

A proton (\( m = 1.67 \times 10^{-27} \) kg, \( q = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \) C) is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 500 V. What is its final speed?

\[ qV = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 \]

\[ v = \sqrt{\frac{2qV}{m}} = \sqrt{\frac{2(1.6 \times 10^{-19})(500)}{1.67 \times 10^{-27}}} = \sqrt{9.58 \times 10^{10}} \approx 3.1 \times 10^5 \text{ m/s} \]

Key Idea: When two charged capacitors are connected, charge redistributes but total charge is conserved. However, energy is NOT conserved — some is always lost as heat in the wires. The final stored energy is always less than the initial total.
AP Exam Tip: The electron-volt is an energy unit, not a voltage unit. Don't confuse 1 eV (energy) with 1 V (potential difference). When converting, \( E(\text{J}) = E(\text{eV}) \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \).

problems.question_html: An electron is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 100 V. What kinetic energy does it gain, in eV?

hints.text: By definition, an electron accelerated through 1 V gains 1 eV.
Through 100 V: \( KE = q\Delta V = (1e)(100 \text{ V}) = 100 \) eV.

problems.question_html: A proton is released from rest in a uniform electric field. It accelerates through a potential difference of 200 V. Which is true about its kinetic energy?

choices.text: It gains 200 eV of kinetic energy
It gains 200 J of kinetic energy
It loses 200 eV of kinetic energy
Its kinetic energy depends on the field strength

hints.text: A charge \( q \) accelerated through \( \Delta V \) gains \( KE = q\Delta V \). A proton has charge \( +1e \).
\( KE = (1e)(200 \text{ V}) = 200 \) eV. The KE depends only on \( q \) and \( \Delta V \), not on the field strength or path.

solution_steps.text: \( KE = q\Delta V \). For a proton (\( q = e \)): \( KE = (1e)(200 \text{ V}) = 200 \) eV.
The kinetic energy gained depends only on the charge and the potential difference, not on the field strength or path taken.

problems.question_html: Convert 500 eV to joules.
A \( +4.0 \) μC charge moves from a point where \( V = 300 \) V to a point where \( V = 100 \) V. How much kinetic energy (in joules) does the charge gain if it starts from rest?

hints.text: \( \Delta KE = q(V_i - V_f) = q\Delta V \) where the charge moves from higher to lower V.

problems.question_html: A proton (\( m = 1.67 \times 10^{-27} \) kg) is accelerated from rest through 1000 V. What is its final speed in m/s?

hints.text: Use energy conservation: \( qV = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 \).

problems.question_html: A 10 μF capacitor charged to 100 V is connected to an uncharged 10 μF capacitor. What is the final voltage across each capacitor, and how much energy is lost?

hints.text: Charge is conserved: \( Q_{\text{total}} = C_1V_1 \). Final: equal V across both (parallel). \( V_f = Q/(C_1+C_2) \).

solution_steps.text: Energy lost: \( 0.05 - 0.025 = 0.025 \) J (dissipated as heat in connecting wires).

problems.question_html: Two identical \( +1.0 \) μC charges are released from rest at a separation of 0.50 m. Each has mass \( 1.0 \times 10^{-3} \) kg. What is the speed of each charge when they are very far apart?

hints.text: Initial PE converts to KE of both charges. By symmetry, each gets half the total KE.
\( U_i = kq^2/r = 0.018 \) J. Each charge gets half: \( \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = 0.009 \) J. \( v = \sqrt{2(0.009)/0.001} = \sqrt{18} \approx 4.2 \) m/s.

solution_steps.text: By symmetry each charge has the same speed: \( 2 \times \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = 0.018 \), so \( mv^2 = 0.018 \).

problems.question_html: An alpha particle (\( q = 3.2 \times 10^{-19} \) C, \( m = 6.64 \times 10^{-27} \) kg) is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 2.0 \times 10^6 V. What is its final speed in m/s?

hints.text: Use \( v = \sqrt{2qV/m} \).

problems.question_html: An electron with initial speed \( 5.0 \times 10^5 \) m/s enters a region where the electric potential increases by 2.0 V. (a) Does the electron speed up or slow down? Explain. (b) Determine the final speed of the electron. (\( m_e = 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \) kg, \( e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \) C.)
problems.sample_answer: (a) For a negative charge, ΔU = qΔV = (−e)(+2.0) = −3.2×10⁻¹⁹ J. PE decreases, so KE increases — the electron speeds up. (b) ΔKE = +3.2×10⁻¹⁹ J. KE_i = ½mv² = ½(9.11×10⁻³¹)(5.0×10⁵)² = 1.14×10⁻¹⁹ J. KE_f = 1.14×10⁻¹⁹ + 3.2×10⁻¹⁹ = 4.34×10⁻¹⁹ J. v_f = √(2×4.34×10⁻¹⁹/9.11×10⁻³¹) ≈ 9.8×10⁵ m/s.
rubric: Correctly identifies that the electron speeds up with valid reasoning about charge sign and PE change (1 point)
Sets up energy conservation correctly with proper signs: ΔKE = −qΔV (1 point)
Correct final speed ≈ 9.8 × 10⁵ m/s with correct calculation (1 point)

hints.text: For a negative charge, moving to higher potential means gaining potential energy (\( U = qV \), and both \( q \) and \( \Delta V \) matter for the sign).
\( \Delta KE = -q\Delta V \). Calculate whether the electron has enough initial KE to overcome the potential increase.

solution_steps.text: (a) For a negative charge, \( \Delta U = q\Delta V = (-e)(+2.0) = -3.2 \times 10^{-19} \) J. PE decreases, so KE increases — the electron speeds up.

problems.correct_answer: (a) For a negative charge, ΔU = qΔV = (−e)(+2.0) = −3.2×10⁻¹⁹ J. PE decreases, so KE increases — the electron speeds up. (b) ΔKE = +3.2×10⁻¹⁹ J. KE_i = ½mv² = ½(9.11×10⁻³¹)(5.0×10⁵)² = 1.14×10⁻¹⁹ J. KE_f = 1.14×10⁻¹⁹ + 3.2×10⁻¹⁹ = 4.34×10⁻¹⁹ J. v_f = √(2×4.34×10⁻¹⁹/9.11×10⁻³¹) ≈ 9.8×10⁵ m/s.
