topics.description: Analyze electric current, simple and compound circuits, resistance, Ohm's law, electric power, Kirchhoff's laws, and RC circuits.

concepts.title: Electric Current
concepts.content_html:
Electric Current

When you flip a light switch, electrons start moving through the wire — that flow of charge is electric current. Current powers everything from smartphones to electric cars.

Definition

Electric current is the rate of charge flow past a point:

\[ I = \frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta t} \]

where:

  • \( I \) = current (amperes, A)
  • \( \Delta Q \) = charge that flows (coulombs, C)
  • \( \Delta t \) = time interval (seconds, s)

1 ampere = 1 coulomb per second.

Conventional Current vs. Electron Flow

Conventional current flows from positive to negative (the direction a positive charge would move). Electron flow is opposite — from negative to positive. Physics and engineering use conventional current by convention.

Drift Velocity

Individual electrons move slowly (\( \sim 10^{-4} \) m/s) — this is the drift velocity. The electric signal, however, travels near the speed of light because the electric field propagates almost instantaneously through the wire.

\[ I = nAv_d \]

where \( n \) = number density of free electrons, \( A \) = cross-sectional area, \( v_d \) = drift velocity.

Key Idea: Current is a scalar quantity — it has magnitude but no direction in the vector sense. However, we assign a direction (conventional current) for circuit analysis purposes.
AP Exam Tip: A common mistake is confusing current with voltage. Current is the flow of charge (like water flow rate); voltage is the energy per charge driving the flow (like water pressure). You can have voltage without current (open circuit) but not sustained current without voltage.

problems.question_html: A wire carries a current of 2.0 A. How much charge passes a point in the wire in 30 seconds?

hints.text: Use \( \Delta Q = I \Delta t \).

problems.question_html: In a metallic conductor, which particles actually move to create the current?

hints.text: In metals, which charged particles are free to move?
Free (valence) electrons move through the metal lattice. Protons are fixed in the nuclei.

solution_steps.text: In metals, the charge carriers are free electrons. They drift through the lattice of positive ions.
Conventional current direction is opposite to electron flow, but electrons are the actual moving charges.

problems.question_html: A current of 0.50 A flows through a wire. How many electrons pass a given point per second? (\( e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \) C)

hints.text: First find the charge per second, then divide by the charge per electron.
\( \Delta Q = 0.50 \) C/s. Number of electrons = \( 0.50 / 1.6 \times 10^{-19} = 3.125 \times 10^{18} \).

solution_steps.text: \( n = \Delta Q / e = 0.50 / 1.6 \times 10^{-19} = 3.125 \times 10^{18} \) electrons per second.

problems.question_html: If 180 C of charge passes through a wire in 1 minute, what is the current in amperes?

hints.text: Convert 1 minute to seconds, then use \( I = \Delta Q / \Delta t \).

problems.question_html: A copper wire has a cross-sectional area of \( 3.0 \times 10^{-6} \) m² and carries a current of 10 A. If copper has \( n = 8.5 \times 10^{28} \) free electrons per m³, what is the drift velocity?

hints.text: Use \( I = nAv_d e \) and solve for \( v_d \).

problems.question_html: A battery delivers a constant current of 0.80 A for 2.5 hours. How much total charge (in coulombs) does it deliver?

hints.text: Convert hours to seconds, then use \( Q = It \).

concepts.title: Simple Circuits
concepts.content_html:
Simple Circuits

A flashlight is one of the simplest circuits: a battery, a switch, a bulb, and wires forming a closed loop. Understanding these basic circuits is the foundation for all electronics.

Circuit Components

  • Battery/EMF source: Provides the energy (EMF, \( \mathcal{E} \)) that drives current. The EMF is the potential difference across the terminals when no current flows.
  • Resistor: Opposes current flow, converting electrical energy to heat.
  • Wire: Assumed to have zero resistance (ideal wire).
  • Switch: Opens or closes the circuit.

Complete Circuit

Current flows only in a closed loop. If any part of the loop is broken (open switch, disconnected wire), current stops everywhere in that loop.

Internal Resistance

Real batteries have internal resistance \( r \). The terminal voltage is less than the EMF when current flows:

\[ V_{\text{terminal}} = \mathcal{E} - Ir \]

where \( I \) is the current drawn from the battery.

Energy in Circuits

The battery does work on charges, increasing their potential energy. As charges flow through resistors, that energy is converted to heat (or light, motion, etc.).

Key Idea: EMF is not a force — it's an energy per unit charge (measured in volts). Think of it as the "pump" that lifts charges to higher potential, analogous to a water pump raising water to a higher elevation.
AP Exam Tip: Internal resistance matters! If a battery has \( \mathcal{E} = 12 \) V and \( r = 1 \) Ω, and delivers 2 A, the terminal voltage is only \( 12 - 2(1) = 10 \) V. The "lost" 2 V appears as heat inside the battery.

problems.question_html: A battery with EMF 9.0 V and internal resistance 0.50 Ω is connected to a 4.0 Ω resistor. What is the current in the circuit?

hints.text: Total resistance = external + internal.

problems.question_html: What is the terminal voltage of the battery in the previous problem?

hints.text: Terminal voltage = EMF − voltage drop across internal resistance.

solution_steps.text: The remaining 1.0 V is "lost" as heat inside the battery.

problems.question_html: A 6.0 V battery with negligible internal resistance is connected to a 12 Ω resistor. What is the current, in amperes?

hints.text: With negligible internal resistance, \( I = V/R \).

problems.question_html: A circuit consists of a switch, a battery, and a light bulb. The switch is open. Is current flowing through the bulb?

hints.text: What does an open switch do to the circuit loop?
An open switch breaks the circuit. No closed loop → no current.

solution_steps.text: An open switch breaks the circuit. Current requires a complete, closed loop to flow. No current flows.

problems.question_html: A battery has an EMF of 12.0 V. When a 5.0 Ω resistor is connected, the terminal voltage is 10.0 V. What is the internal resistance of the battery?

hints.text: First find the current using \( I = V_{\text{terminal}}/R \), then use \( V = \mathcal{E} - Ir \).

problems.question_html: A 9.0 V battery with internal resistance 0.30 Ω delivers 3.0 A. What fraction of the total power is dissipated internally?

hints.text: Power dissipated internally: \( P_r = I^2 r \). Total power: \( P = \mathcal{E} I \).

concepts.title: Resistance, Resistivity, and Ohm's Law
concepts.content_html:
Resistance, Resistivity, and Ohm's Law

Why does a thin wire get hotter than a thick wire carrying the same current? Why are copper wires used instead of iron? The answers involve resistance and resistivity.

Ohm's Law

For many materials, the current through a conductor is proportional to the voltage across it:

\[ V = IR \]

where:

  • \( V \) = voltage (V)
  • \( I \) = current (A)
  • \( R \) = resistance (ohms, Ω)

Materials that obey this linear relationship are called ohmic.

Resistivity

Resistance depends on the material and geometry:

\[ R = \frac{\rho L}{A} \]

where:

  • \( \rho \) = resistivity (Ω·m) — a material property
  • \( L \) = length of the conductor (m)
  • \( A \) = cross-sectional area (m²)

Metals have low resistivity (\( \sim 10^{-8} \) Ω·m); insulators have high resistivity (\( \sim 10^{10} \) Ω·m).

Temperature Dependence

For most metals, resistivity increases with temperature. As the metal heats up, lattice vibrations increase, impeding electron flow.

Key Idea: Doubling the length of a wire doubles its resistance. Doubling the cross-sectional area halves its resistance. Think of it like water in a pipe: longer pipe = more friction; wider pipe = easier flow.
AP Exam Tip: Not all devices are ohmic. Light bulbs, diodes, and semiconductors do not obey Ohm's law (their \( V \)-\( I \) graph is not a straight line). The AP exam may ask you to identify ohmic vs. non-ohmic behavior from a graph.

problem_sets.title: Practice: Resistance, Resistivity, and Ohm's Law

problems.question_html: A resistor has a voltage of 12 V across it and carries a current of 3.0 A. What is its resistance?

hints.text: Use Ohm's law: \( R = V/I \).

problems.question_html: A copper wire has a resistivity of \( 1.7 \times 10^{-8} \) Ω·m, length 2.0 m, and cross-sectional area \( 1.0 \times 10^{-6} \) m². What is its resistance?

hints.text: Use \( R = \rho L / A \).

problems.question_html: What current flows through a 100 Ω resistor connected to a 9.0 V battery? Give your answer in amperes.
A wire of length \( L \) and cross-sectional area \( A \) has resistance \( R \). If the wire is stretched to twice its original length (keeping volume constant), what is the new resistance?

hints.text: Volume = \( LA \) = constant. If \( L \to 2L \), then \( A \to A/2 \).
New \( R = \rho(2L)/(A/2) = 4\rho L/A = 4R \).

solution_steps.text: Volume constant: \( LA = 2L \cdot A' \), so \( A' = A/2 \).

problem_sets.title: Premium: Resistance, Resistivity, and Ohm's Law

problems.question_html: Two wires are made of the same material. Wire A has twice the length and three times the cross-sectional area of Wire B. What is the ratio \( R_A / R_B \)?

hints.text: \( R = \rho L/A \). Same \( \rho \).

problems.question_html: A nichrome wire (\( \rho = 1.1 \times 10^{-6} \) Ω·m) is used in a heater. If the wire is 5.0 m long and has a diameter of 0.50 mm, what is its resistance? Round to the nearest ohm.

hints.text: \( A = \pi (d/2)^2 \). Then \( R = \rho L / A \).

problems.question_html: A student measures the voltage across and current through a device at several settings. The V-I data is: (2V, 0.1A), (4V, 0.2A), (6V, 0.3A), (8V, 0.4A). Is this device ohmic? What is its resistance?

hints.text: Check if \( V/I \) is constant. If so, the device is ohmic.

solution_steps.text: \( V/I \) at each point: 20, 20, 20, 20 Ω. Constant ratio → ohmic.

problems.question_html: A wire of resistivity \( \rho \), length \( L \), and radius \( r \) has resistance \( R \). A second wire of the same material has length \( 2L \) and radius \( 2r \). Derive the resistance of the second wire in terms of \( R \), and explain how both length and radius affect resistance.
problems.sample_answer: R₁ = ρL/(πr²). R₂ = ρ(2L)/(π(2r)²) = 2ρL/(4πr²) = ρL/(2πr²) = R/2. Doubling the length doubles resistance, but doubling the radius quadruples the area, which quarters the resistance. Net effect: R₂ = R/2.
rubric: Correctly applies R = ρL/A with A = πr² for both wires (1 point)
Arrives at R₂ = R/2 (1 point)
Explains the competing effects of length (doubles R) and area (quarters R) (1 point)

hints.text: \( R = \rho L / A \) where \( A = \pi r^2 \).
Doubling \( r \) quadruples \( A \). How does that combine with doubling \( L \)?

solution_steps.text: Length effect: \( 2L \to 2R \). Radius effect: \( 2r \to A \times 4 \to R/4 \). Combined: \( 2 \times (1/4) = 1/2 \). \( R_2 = R/2 \).

problems.correct_answer: R₁ = ρL/(πr²). R₂ = ρ(2L)/(π(2r)²) = 2ρL/(4πr²) = ρL/(2πr²) = R/2. Doubling the length doubles resistance, but doubling the radius quadruples the area, which quarters the resistance. Net effect: R₂ = R/2.

concepts.title: Electric Power
concepts.content_html:
Electric Power

Your electricity bill charges by the kilowatt-hour — a measure of energy. Understanding electric power helps you calculate how much energy devices consume and why some circuits overheat.

Power Equations

Electric power is the rate of energy transfer:

\[ P = IV \]

Using Ohm's law (\( V = IR \)), we get two more forms:

\[ P = I^2R = \frac{V^2}{R} \]

where:

  • \( P \) = power (watts, W)
  • \( I \) = current (A)
  • \( V \) = voltage (V)
  • \( R \) = resistance (Ω)

Energy

Energy consumed over time:

\[ E = Pt \]

The kilowatt-hour (kWh) is a common energy unit: 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J.

Power Dissipation in Resistors

In a resistor, electrical energy is converted to thermal energy (heat). A 100 W light bulb converts 100 joules of electrical energy to light and heat every second.

Key Idea: Use \( P = I^2R \) when you know current and resistance. Use \( P = V^2/R \) when you know voltage and resistance. These give different results for the same resistor only if you're confused about whether the voltage or current is the independent variable.
AP Exam Tip: In series circuits, the same current flows through all resistors, so use \( P = I^2R \) — the resistor with the highest \( R \) dissipates the most power. In parallel circuits, all resistors have the same voltage, so use \( P = V^2/R \) — the resistor with the lowest \( R \) dissipates the most power.

problems.question_html: A 60 W light bulb operates at 120 V. What current does it draw?
A 10 Ω resistor carries a current of 3.0 A. How much power does it dissipate?

hints.text: Use \( P = I^2R \) when current and resistance are known.

problems.question_html: A 1500 W heater runs for 2 hours. How much energy does it consume, in kWh?

hints.text: Energy = Power × time. Express power in kW and time in hours.
\( E = 1.5 \text{ kW} \times 2 \text{ h} = 3 \) kWh.

problems.question_html: A 200 Ω resistor is connected to a 100 V source. What power does it dissipate, in watts?

hints.text: Use \( P = V^2/R \).

problems.question_html: Two resistors, 4 Ω and 12 Ω, are connected in series to a 24 V battery. Which resistor dissipates more power, and how much?

hints.text: In series, the current is the same through both. Use \( P = I^2R \). Higher \( R \) gets more power.

solution_steps.text: Total \( R = 16 \) Ω. \( I = 24/16 = 1.5 \) A (same through both).
The 12 Ω resistor dissipates 27 W — in series, larger \( R \) gets more power.

problems.question_html: Two resistors, 4 Ω and 12 Ω, are connected in parallel to a 24 V battery. Which dissipates more power?

hints.text: In parallel, voltage is the same. Use \( P = V^2/R \). Lower \( R \) gets more power.
\( P_4 = 24^2/4 = 144 \) W. \( P_{12} = 24^2/12 = 48 \) W. The 4 Ω resistor dissipates more.

solution_steps.text: Same voltage across both: \( P = V^2/R \).
\( P_4 = 576/4 = 144 \) W. \( P_{12} = 576/12 = 48 \) W. The 4 Ω resistor gets three times the power.

problems.question_html: A household circuit breaker trips at 15 A. If the circuit operates at 120 V, what is the maximum power (in watts) that can be drawn from this circuit?

hints.text: \( P_{\text{max}} = I_{\text{max}} \times V \).

problems.question_html: A student connects a resistor to a variable power supply. At 6 V, the current is 0.30 A and the power is 1.8 W. At 12 V, the current is 0.55 A and the power is 6.6 W. (a) Is this resistor ohmic? Justify. (b) Calculate the resistance at each voltage.
problems.sample_answer: (a) R at 6V = V/I = 6/0.30 = 20 Ω. R at 12V = 12/0.55 = 21.8 Ω. Since R changes, the device is NOT perfectly ohmic (though close). An ohmic device has constant R. (b) R₁ = 20 Ω at 6 V; R₂ ≈ 21.8 Ω at 12 V.
rubric: Calculates R at both voltages (1 point)
Correctly identifies non-ohmic behavior because R is not constant (1 point)
Provides both resistance values with units (1 point)

hints.text: An ohmic device has constant \( R = V/I \) at all voltages.
Calculate \( R \) at each voltage and compare.

solution_steps.text: Since \( R \) changes with voltage (20 Ω vs 21.8 Ω), the device is not perfectly ohmic.
Likely a light bulb or similar device where resistance increases with temperature.

problems.correct_answer: (a) R at 6V = V/I = 6/0.30 = 20 Ω. R at 12V = 12/0.55 = 21.8 Ω. Since R changes, the device is NOT perfectly ohmic (though close). An ohmic device has constant R. (b) R₁ = 20 Ω at 6 V; R₂ ≈ 21.8 Ω at 12 V.

concepts.title: Compound Direct Current (DC) Circuits
concepts.content_html:
Compound Direct Current (DC) Circuits

Most real circuits aren't purely series or purely parallel — they're compound circuits with combinations of both. Analyzing these requires systematically reducing the circuit to simpler equivalents.

Series Resistors

\[ R_{\text{eq}} = R_1 + R_2 + R_3 + \cdots \]

Same current through each. Voltages add up to the total.

Parallel Resistors

\[ \frac{1}{R_{\text{eq}}} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} + \frac{1}{R_3} + \cdots \]

Same voltage across each. Currents add up to the total. For two resistors: \( R_{\text{eq}} = R_1 R_2/(R_1 + R_2) \).

Analyzing Compound Circuits

  1. Identify groups of resistors that are purely in series or purely in parallel.
  2. Replace each group with its equivalent resistance.
  3. Repeat until the circuit is reduced to a single equivalent resistance.
  4. Find the total current from \( I = V/R_{\text{eq}} \).
  5. Work backwards to find individual voltages and currents.

Ammeter and Voltmeter

An ammeter measures current — connected in series, it has very low resistance. A voltmeter measures voltage — connected in parallel, it has very high resistance.

Key Idea: In series, current is the same; voltage divides. In parallel, voltage is the same; current divides. This is the foundation of all circuit analysis.
AP Exam Tip: When a resistor is removed from a parallel combination, the equivalent resistance increases, total current decreases, and the voltage across remaining parallel resistors stays the same (if connected to an ideal battery). The exam loves these qualitative questions.

problems.question_html: Three resistors of 2 Ω, 3 Ω, and 5 Ω are connected in series. What is the equivalent resistance?

hints.text: Series: \( R_{\text{eq}} = R_1 + R_2 + R_3 \).

problems.question_html: Two resistors, 6 Ω and 3 Ω, are connected in parallel. What is the equivalent resistance?

hints.text: For two resistors in parallel: \( R_{\text{eq}} = R_1 R_2/(R_1 + R_2) \).

problems.question_html: A 4 Ω resistor is in series with a parallel combination of 6 Ω and 12 Ω. What is the total equivalent resistance, in Ω?

hints.text: First find the parallel equivalent, then add the series resistor.

problems.question_html: In the circuit above (4 Ω in series with 6 Ω ∥ 12 Ω), connected to a 24 V battery, what is the current through the 6 Ω resistor, in amperes?

hints.text: Find total current first, then the voltage across the parallel section, then split the current.
Total \( I = 24/8 = 3 \) A. Voltage across parallel: \( V_p = IR_p = 3(4) = 12 \) V. Current through 6 Ω: \( I_6 = 12/6 = 2 \) A.

solution_steps.text: Voltage across the parallel combo: \( V_p = I \times R_p = 3 \times 4 = 12 \) V.

problems.question_html: Three 12 Ω resistors are connected: two in parallel, and that combination in series with the third. Connected to a 12 V battery, what is the total current?

solution_steps.text: Two 12 Ω in parallel: \( R_p = 6 \) Ω. In series with 12 Ω: \( R_{\text{eq}} = 18 \) Ω.

problems.question_html: A circuit has a 10 Ω and a 15 Ω resistor in parallel. This combination is in series with a 4 Ω resistor and a 30 V battery. What is the voltage across the parallel combination?

hints.text: Find \( R_p \), then \( R_{\text{eq}} \), then \( I \), then \( V_p = IR_p \).

problems.question_html: A light bulb rated at 100 W, 120 V is connected to a 120 V source. A second identical bulb is then connected in series with the first (still 120 V source). Does each bulb get brighter or dimmer compared to a single bulb? Explain.

choices.text: One gets brighter and one gets dimmer

hints.text: Each bulb has \( R = V^2/P = 144 \) Ω. In series, total \( R \) doubles, so total current decreases.
With one bulb: \( I = 120/144 = 0.83 \) A, \( P = 100 \) W. With two in series: \( I = 120/288 = 0.42 \) A. Each gets \( P = I^2R = (0.42)^2(144) = 25 \) W — much dimmer.

solution_steps.text: Each bulb: \( P = I^2R = (0.417)^2(144) = 25 \) W. Much dimmer (25 W vs 100 W).

problems.question_html: In a circuit, a voltmeter reads 8.0 V across a 20 Ω resistor. What is the current through the resistor, in amperes?

hints.text: A voltmeter measures the voltage across the resistor. Use Ohm's law.

problems.question_html: A 48 V battery is connected to three resistors: \( R_1 = 8 \) Ω in series with a parallel combination of \( R_2 = 12 \) Ω and \( R_3 = 24 \) Ω. Determine the current through each resistor and the power dissipated by \( R_2 \).
rubric: Correctly calculates equivalent resistance and total current: R_eq = 16 Ω, I = 3 A (1 point)
Correctly finds individual currents: I₂ = 2 A, I₃ = 1 A (1 point)
Correctly calculates power dissipated by R₂: P₂ = 48 W (1 point)

hints.text: Find \( R_p \) for the parallel pair, then \( R_{\text{eq}} \), then work backwards.

concepts.title: Kirchhoff's Loop Rule
concepts.content_html:
Kirchhoff's Loop Rule

Kirchhoff's loop rule is the energy conservation law applied to circuits. It says that as you travel around any closed loop in a circuit, the total change in electric potential is zero — you end up where you started.

The Rule

\[ \sum \Delta V = 0 \quad \text{(around any closed loop)} \]

This means: the sum of all EMF gains equals the sum of all voltage drops across resistors.

Sign Conventions

  • Traversing a battery from − to +: \( +\mathcal{E} \) (voltage gain).
  • Traversing a battery from + to −: \( -\mathcal{E} \) (voltage drop).
  • Traversing a resistor in the direction of current: \( -IR \) (voltage drop).
  • Traversing a resistor against the current: \( +IR \) (voltage gain).

Applying the Loop Rule

  1. Assign a direction of current (guess if needed — if you get a negative answer, the actual direction is opposite).
  2. Choose a loop direction (clockwise or counterclockwise).
  3. Walk around the loop, writing \( +\mathcal{E} \) or \( -\mathcal{E} \) for batteries and \( \pm IR \) for resistors.
  4. Set the sum equal to zero and solve.
Key Idea: The loop rule works because electric potential is path-independent. No matter what path you take around a loop, you must return to the same potential you started at — just like returning to the same elevation after walking around a hill.
AP Exam Tip: When a problem has multiple batteries or complex circuits that can't be simplified to series/parallel, you need Kirchhoff's rules. Write one equation per loop and one per junction (next topic). The number of independent equations must equal the number of unknown currents.

problems.question_html: A simple loop has a 12 V battery and two resistors (4 Ω and 8 Ω) in series. Using the loop rule, find the current.

hints.text: Loop rule: \( \mathcal{E} - IR_1 - IR_2 = 0 \).
\( 12 - 4I - 8I = 0 \Rightarrow 12I = 12 \Rightarrow I = 1.0 \) A.

problems.question_html: A loop contains a 9 V battery and a 6 V battery (opposing each other) with a 6 Ω resistor. What is the current?

hints.text: Opposing batteries: the net EMF is \( 9 - 6 = 3 \) V.
\( I = (9 - 6)/6 = 3/6 = 0.50 \) A, driven by the larger battery.

solution_steps.text: Loop rule: \( +9 - 6 - 6I = 0 \) (traversing in direction of current from larger battery).

problems.question_html: A circuit loop contains a 20 V battery and three resistors. The voltage drops across two of them are 8 V and 5 V. What is the voltage drop across the third resistor, in volts?

hints.text: By the loop rule, all voltage drops must sum to the EMF.

problems.question_html: In a single-loop circuit with a 15 V battery and three resistors in series (3 Ω, 5 Ω, 7 Ω), what is the voltage drop across the 5 Ω resistor, in volts?

hints.text: Find the total current first, then \( V = IR \) for the 5 Ω.

problems.question_html: Two batteries, \( \mathcal{E}_1 = 12 \) V and \( \mathcal{E}_2 = 8 \) V, are connected in the same direction with a 10 Ω resistor in the loop. What is the current?

hints.text: Same direction → EMFs add.

problems.question_html: A circuit has two loops sharing a common resistor. The left loop has a 10 V battery and resistors 2 Ω and 3 Ω (the shared one). The right loop has a 6 V battery and resistors 3 Ω (shared) and 4 Ω. Using the loop rule for the left loop (assuming current \( I_1 \) through the left and \( I_2 \) through the right), write the loop equation.

hints.text: The shared 3 Ω resistor carries current \( I_1 - I_2 \) (difference of the two loop currents).
Left loop: battery gives +10 V, then drops \( 2I_1 \) and \( 3(I_1 - I_2) \).

solution_steps.text: In the left loop (clockwise), traversing: \( +10 - 2I_1 - 3(I_1 - I_2) = 0 \).
The shared resistor carries \( I_1 - I_2 \) because both loop currents pass through it but in potentially different directions.

problems.question_html: A single loop has a 24 V battery with internal resistance 1 Ω and an external resistance of 11 Ω. What voltage does a voltmeter read across the battery terminals?

hints.text: Loop rule: \( \mathcal{E} - Ir - IR = 0 \). The terminal voltage is \( \mathcal{E} - Ir \).

problems.question_html: A circuit has two batteries (\( \mathcal{E}_1 = 18 \) V, \( r_1 = 1 \) Ω and \( \mathcal{E}_2 = 12 \) V, \( r_2 = 2 \) Ω) opposing each other, with an external resistor \( R = 3 \) Ω. Use the loop rule to find the current and determine which battery is charging.
problems.sample_answer: Loop: +18 − 1·I − 3·I − 12 − 2·I = 0 → 6 = 6I → I = 1.0 A. Current flows from the 18 V battery through the circuit. The 12 V battery is being charged (current enters its positive terminal).
rubric: Correctly writes the loop equation with proper signs (1 point)
Solves for I = 1.0 A (1 point)
Identifies that the 12 V battery is being charged with correct reasoning (1 point)

hints.text: Assume current flows in the direction driven by the larger EMF.

solution_steps.text: Assume current flows counterclockwise (driven by 18 V battery).
Current enters the + terminal of the 12 V battery → it is being charged. The 18 V battery drives the circuit.

problems.correct_answer: Loop: +18 − 1·I − 3·I − 12 − 2·I = 0 → 6 = 6I → I = 1.0 A. Current flows from the 18 V battery through the circuit. The 12 V battery is being charged (current enters its positive terminal).

concepts.title: Kirchhoff's Junction Rule
concepts.content_html:
Kirchhoff's Junction Rule

At any junction (node) in a circuit, charge is conserved — what flows in must flow out. This is Kirchhoff's junction rule, the charge conservation law applied to circuits.

The Rule

\[ \sum I_{\text{in}} = \sum I_{\text{out}} \]

The total current entering a junction equals the total current leaving that junction.

Application

At a junction where a wire splits into two branches:

\[ I_{\text{total}} = I_1 + I_2 \]

This is how current divides at parallel branches — each branch gets a portion of the total current inversely proportional to its resistance.

Current Divider

For two resistors in parallel with total current \( I \):

\[ I_1 = I \cdot \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}, \quad I_2 = I \cdot \frac{R_1}{R_1 + R_2} \]

More current flows through the path of least resistance.

Key Idea: The junction rule is just conservation of charge. Charge doesn't accumulate at a junction in steady state — every coulomb that arrives must leave. This is true at every instant, for any circuit.
AP Exam Tip: In multi-loop circuit problems, combine the junction rule with the loop rule. Assign current variables to each branch. Write junction equations at nodes where branches meet. Write loop equations for independent loops. Solve the system of equations.

problems.question_html: At a junction, 5.0 A enters from one wire and the current splits into two branches. If one branch carries 3.0 A, what current flows in the other branch?

hints.text: Junction rule: current in = current out.

problems.question_html: Three wires meet at a junction. Wire A carries 4 A into the junction, Wire B carries 6 A into the junction. What current flows out through Wire C?

hints.text: Sum of currents in = sum of currents out.

solution_steps.text: \( I_C = I_A + I_B = 4 + 6 = 10 \) A flowing out of the junction.

problems.question_html: A 12 A current splits into two parallel branches. One branch has 4 Ω and the other has 12 Ω. What current flows through the 4 Ω branch?

hints.text: Use the current divider: \( I_1 = I \cdot R_2/(R_1 + R_2) \).

problems.question_html: At a junction, three currents meet: 2 A flows in, 5 A flows in, and an unknown current \( I_3 \) flows out. A fourth wire also exits with 3 A. What is \( I_3 \)?

hints.text: \( \sum I_{\text{in}} = \sum I_{\text{out}} \).

problems.question_html: Three resistors (2 Ω, 4 Ω, 6 Ω) are connected in parallel to a 12 V battery. What is the total current supplied by the battery?

hints.text: Each branch has 12 V. Find each branch current and add (junction rule).

problems.question_html: In a Wheatstone bridge, if \( R_1 = 100 \) Ω, \( R_2 = 200 \) Ω, \( R_3 = 300 \) Ω, and \( R_4 \) is unknown, what value of \( R_4 \) balances the bridge (zero current through the galvanometer)?

hints.text: A balanced Wheatstone bridge: \( R_1/R_2 = R_3/R_4 \).

problems.question_html: Two 6 Ω resistors are in parallel, and this combination is in series with a 3 Ω resistor. If the total current from the battery is 4 A, what is the current through each 6 Ω resistor?

hints.text: The 4 A total current flows through the series 3 Ω, then splits equally at the parallel junction (identical resistors).
Equal resistors split current equally: \( 4/2 = 2 \) A each.

solution_steps.text: Both 6 Ω resistors are identical and in parallel → current splits equally.

problems.question_html: A circuit has a 24 V battery and three branches in parallel: Branch A has 8 Ω, Branch B has 12 Ω, and Branch C has 24 Ω. Using both Kirchhoff's rules, find the current in each branch and verify that the junction rule is satisfied.
problems.sample_answer: Each branch has 24 V across it. I_A = 24/8 = 3 A. I_B = 24/12 = 2 A. I_C = 24/24 = 1 A. Junction: I_total = 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 A entering = 6 A leaving ✓. Loop check: 24 - 8(3) = 24 - 24 = 0 ✓.
rubric: Correctly calculates all three branch currents (1 point)
Verifies junction rule: sum of branch currents = total current (1 point)
Verifies loop rule for at least one loop (1 point)

hints.text: In parallel, each branch has the full battery voltage.
\( I = V/R \) for each branch. Then check \( I_A + I_B + I_C = I_{\text{total}} \).

problems.correct_answer: Each branch has 24 V across it. I_A = 24/8 = 3 A. I_B = 24/12 = 2 A. I_C = 24/24 = 1 A. Junction: I_total = 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 A entering = 6 A leaving ✓. Loop check: 24 - 8(3) = 24 - 24 = 0 ✓.

concepts.title: Resistor-Capacitor (RC) Circuits
concepts.content_html:
Resistor-Capacitor (RC) Circuits

When you take a photo with a flash, the flash capacitor charges slowly through a resistor, then discharges rapidly through the flash tube. This charging and discharging behavior is governed by RC circuits.

Time Constant

The time constant \( \tau \) determines how quickly a capacitor charges or discharges:

\[ \tau = RC \]

where \( R \) is the resistance (Ω) and \( C \) is the capacitance (F). After one time constant, the capacitor has charged to about 63% of its maximum (or discharged to about 37% of its initial value).

Charging a Capacitor

When a battery charges a capacitor through a resistor:

  • Voltage across capacitor: \( V_C(t) = \mathcal{E}(1 - e^{-t/RC}) \)
  • Current: \( I(t) = \frac{\mathcal{E}}{R} e^{-t/RC} \)

Initially (\( t = 0 \)): \( V_C = 0 \), \( I = \mathcal{E}/R \) (maximum current). After a long time: \( V_C = \mathcal{E} \), \( I = 0 \).

Discharging a Capacitor

  • Voltage: \( V_C(t) = V_0 e^{-t/RC} \)
  • Current: \( I(t) = \frac{V_0}{R} e^{-t/RC} \)

Both decay exponentially to zero.

Qualitative Behavior (No Calculus Needed)

For the AP exam, focus on:

  • At \( t = 0 \): an uncharged capacitor acts like a wire (short circuit); a fully charged capacitor acts like an open circuit (no current).
  • At \( t \to \infty \): the capacitor is fully charged, current stops.
  • Larger \( R \) or \( C \) means slower charging/discharging.
Key Idea: After about \( 5\tau \), the capacitor is considered fully charged (\( > 99\% \)). The time constant \( \tau = RC \) is the single number that characterizes how fast the circuit responds.
AP Exam Tip: You won't need to evaluate exponentials on the AP exam. Focus on the limiting cases (\( t = 0 \) and \( t \to \infty \)), the meaning of the time constant, and how changing \( R \) or \( C \) affects the behavior. Know that current starts high and decays during charging, and that voltage across the capacitor grows from 0 to \( \mathcal{E} \).

problems.question_html: An RC circuit has \( R = 1000 \) Ω and \( C = 500 \) μF. What is the time constant?

hints.text: \( \tau = RC \). Watch the units: μF = \( 10^{-6} \) F.

problems.question_html: An uncharged capacitor is connected in series with a resistor and a battery. At \( t = 0 \), what is the current?

hints.text: At \( t = 0 \), the uncharged capacitor has \( V_C = 0 \), so it acts like a wire.
All the battery voltage drops across the resistor: \( I = \mathcal{E}/R \).

solution_steps.text: At \( t = 0 \): \( V_C = 0 \), so the capacitor is like a short circuit.
The full EMF drives current through \( R \): \( I_0 = \mathcal{E}/R \) (maximum current).

problems.question_html: After a very long time, a charging RC circuit reaches steady state. What is the current through the circuit?

hints.text: A fully charged capacitor acts like an open circuit.
When \( V_C = \mathcal{E} \), there is no net driving voltage. Current = 0.

solution_steps.text: At \( t \to \infty \), the capacitor is fully charged to \( V_C = \mathcal{E} \).
No potential difference remains to drive current, so \( I = 0 \).

problems.question_html: If the resistance in an RC circuit is doubled, how does the time constant change?

hints.text: \( \tau = RC \). If \( R \to 2R \), what happens to \( \tau \)?
\( \tau' = 2RC = 2\tau \). The time constant doubles.

solution_steps.text: \( \tau = RC \). Doubling \( R \): \( \tau' = 2RC = 2\tau \). The time constant doubles, meaning the circuit charges/discharges more slowly.

problems.question_html: A 10 V battery charges a 100 μF capacitor through a 2000 Ω resistor. What is the initial current, and what fraction of the maximum voltage is on the capacitor after one time constant?

hints.text: Initial current \( I_0 = \mathcal{E}/R \). After one \( \tau \), voltage is about 63% of max.

solution_steps.text: After one time constant (\( \tau = RC = 0.20 \) s), the capacitor has charged to \( 1 - 1/e \approx 63\% \) of \( \mathcal{E} \).

problems.question_html: A charged RC circuit is discharging. The initial voltage is 24 V and the time constant is 2.0 s. After 2.0 seconds, approximately what percentage of the initial voltage remains on the capacitor?

hints.text: After one time constant, the voltage drops to \( 1/e \) of the initial value.
\( V = V_0 e^{-1} \approx 0.37 V_0 \). About 37% remains.

solution_steps.text: After \( t = \tau \): \( V = V_0 e^{-t/\tau} = V_0 e^{-1} \approx 0.37 V_0 \).
About 37% of the initial voltage remains (\( \approx 8.8 \) V out of 24 V).

problems.question_html: A fully charged 50 μF capacitor at 20 V is discharged through a 4000 Ω resistor. After how many time constants has the voltage dropped to about 5 V?

hints.text: \( V = V_0 e^{-t/\tau} \). \( 5 = 20 e^{-t/\tau} \). Solve for \( t/\tau \).

problems.question_html: An RC circuit has \( R = 5000 \) Ω and \( C = 200 \) μF. What is the time constant in seconds?

hints.text: \( \tau = RC \).

problems.question_html: An uncharged 100 μF capacitor is connected to a 12 V battery through a 10 kΩ resistor. (a) What is the time constant? (b) Describe qualitatively how the current and voltage across the capacitor change with time. (c) What is the energy stored in the capacitor when fully charged?
problems.sample_answer: (a) τ = RC = (10000)(100 × 10⁻⁶) = 1.0 s. (b) At t = 0: current is maximum (I₀ = 12/10000 = 1.2 mA), V_C = 0. Over time, current decreases exponentially while V_C increases exponentially toward 12 V. After ~5τ = 5 s, current ≈ 0 and V_C ≈ 12 V. (c) U = ½CV² = ½(100 × 10⁻⁶)(12)² = 7.2 × 10⁻³ J = 7.2 mJ.
rubric: Correct time constant: τ = 1.0 s (1 point)
Correctly describes exponential behavior of both current (decreasing) and voltage (increasing) (1 point)
Correct energy: U = 7.2 mJ (1 point)

hints.text: \( \tau = RC \). At \( t = 0 \), capacitor is a wire. At \( t \to \infty \), capacitor is open.
Energy stored: \( U = \frac{1}{2}CV^2 \) when fully charged to \( V = \mathcal{E} \).

solution_steps.text: (b) Current starts at \( I_0 = 12/10000 = 1.2 \) mA and decays exponentially. \( V_C \) starts at 0 and grows exponentially toward 12 V. After \( 5\tau = 5 \) s, charging is essentially complete.

problems.correct_answer: (a) τ = RC = (10000)(100 × 10⁻⁶) = 1.0 s. (b) At t = 0: current is maximum (I₀ = 12/10000 = 1.2 mA), V_C = 0. Over time, current decreases exponentially while V_C increases exponentially toward 12 V. After ~5τ = 5 s, current ≈ 0 and V_C ≈ 12 V. (c) U = ½CV² = ½(100 × 10⁻⁶)(12)² = 7.2 × 10⁻³ J = 7.2 mJ.
