Moving the source vs. moving the observer gives different formulas because the medium provides an absolute reference frame. For light, there is no medium — light travels through vacuum. The Doppler effect for light depends only on the relative velocity between source and observer, not on any medium. Also, for light at high speeds, relativistic effects must be considered.

concepts.title: Wave Interference and Standing Waves
concepts.content_html:
Wave Interference and Standing Waves

When two waves overlap, they interfere. If they reinforce each other, it's constructive interference. If they cancel, it's destructive interference. A special case: two identical waves traveling in opposite directions create a standing wave.

Constructive and Destructive Interference

  • Constructive: waves in phase (crest meets crest) → larger amplitude. Path difference = \( 0, \lambda, 2\lambda, ... = m\lambda \)
  • Destructive: waves out of phase (crest meets trough) → smaller or zero amplitude. Path difference = \( \lambda/2, 3\lambda/2, ... = (m + \frac{1}{2})\lambda \)

Standing Waves on a String

A string fixed at both ends can vibrate at specific frequencies called harmonics:

\[ f_n = n \cdot \frac{v}{2L} = n f_1 \quad (n = 1, 2, 3, ...) \]

where \( L \) = string length, \( v \) = wave speed, and \( n \) = harmonic number.

  • \( n = 1 \): fundamental (1st harmonic) — 1 antinode, 2 nodes
  • \( n = 2 \): 2nd harmonic — 2 antinodes, 3 nodes
  • The \( n \)th harmonic has \( n \) antinodes and \( n + 1 \) nodes

Standing Waves in Open and Closed Pipes

  • Open pipe (open at both ends): all harmonics. \( f_n = nv/(2L) \)
  • Closed pipe (one end closed): only odd harmonics. \( f_n = nv/(4L) \), \( n = 1, 3, 5, ... \)
Key Idea: Nodes are points of zero displacement. Antinodes are points of maximum displacement. Fixed ends are always nodes; open ends are always antinodes.
AP Exam Tip: A pipe closed at one end produces only odd harmonics (1st, 3rd, 5th...). This is a very common exam question. The fundamental has \( \lambda = 4L \) for a closed pipe vs. \( \lambda = 2L \) for an open pipe.

problems.question_html: Two waves interfere constructively when the path difference between them is:

hints.text: Constructive = crests align. What path difference produces this?
Constructive interference: path difference = integer multiple of wavelength: \( 0, \lambda, 2\lambda, 3\lambda, ... \).

solution_steps.text: Constructive interference occurs when the path difference is \( m\lambda \) (\( m = 0, 1, 2, ... \)). Crests arrive together.

problems.question_html: A guitar string of length 0.60 m vibrates in its fundamental mode. What is the wavelength of the standing wave?

hints.text: For the fundamental on a string fixed at both ends, the string length is half a wavelength.

problems.question_html: A pipe open at both ends has a length of 0.85 m. What is its fundamental frequency? (\( v_{\text{sound}} = 340 \) m/s). Round to the nearest whole number.

hints.text: Open pipe: \( f_1 = v/(2L) \).

problems.question_html: A pipe closed at one end and open at the other has a length of 0.50 m. What is its fundamental frequency? (\( v = 340 \) m/s). Round to the nearest whole number.

hints.text: Closed pipe: \( f_1 = v/(4L) \).

problems.question_html: A pipe closed at one end produces a fundamental at 170 Hz. What is the frequency of the next harmonic it can produce?

hints.text: A closed pipe only produces odd harmonics.
Odd harmonics only: 1st (170 Hz), 3rd (510 Hz), 5th (850 Hz)... Next after fundamental is 3rd harmonic = \( 3 \times 170 = 510 \) Hz.

problems.question_html: A string vibrating in its 3rd harmonic has how many nodes and antinodes?

hints.text: The \( n \)th harmonic has \( n \) antinodes. How many nodes?
3rd harmonic: 3 antinodes and \( n + 1 = 4 \) nodes (including the two fixed ends).

solution_steps.text: The \( n \)th harmonic has \( n \) antinodes and \( n + 1 \) nodes.

problems.question_html: A string of length 1.0 m has a wave speed of 200 m/s. What is the frequency of the 4th harmonic, in Hz?
A tube is initially open at both ends and has a fundamental frequency of 300 Hz. If one end is now closed, what is the new fundamental frequency?
problems.sample_answer: Open pipe: f₁ = v/(2L) = 300 Hz. So v/(2L) = 300, meaning v = 600L. Closed pipe: f₁ = v/(4L) = 600L/(4L) = 150 Hz. The fundamental frequency is halved to 150 Hz. This is because the closed pipe has a wavelength of 4L (vs. 2L for open), so the fundamental wavelength doubles, and frequency halves.
rubric: Uses the open pipe formula to relate v and L (1 point)
Applies the closed pipe formula correctly to find f₁ = v/(4L) = 150 Hz (1 point)
Explains that closing one end doubles the fundamental wavelength, halving the frequency (1 point)

hints.text: Open pipe: \( f_1 = v/(2L) \). Closed pipe: \( f_1 = v/(4L) \). The same \( v \) and \( L \).

solution_steps.text: Closing one end halves the fundamental frequency (wavelength doubles from \( 2L \) to \( 4L \)).

problems.correct_answer: Open pipe: f₁ = v/(2L) = 300 Hz. So v/(2L) = 300, meaning v = 600L. Closed pipe: f₁ = v/(4L) = 600L/(4L) = 150 Hz. The fundamental frequency is halved to 150 Hz. This is because the closed pipe has a wavelength of 4L (vs. 2L for open), so the fundamental wavelength doubles, and frequency halves.

concepts.title: Diffraction
concepts.content_html:
Diffraction

When a wave passes through an opening or around an obstacle, it bends and spreads out — this is diffraction. It's the reason you can hear someone around a corner even though you can't see them (sound diffracts more than light because of its longer wavelength).

When Does Diffraction Occur?

Diffraction is most noticeable when the wavelength is comparable to the size of the opening or obstacle:

  • \( \lambda \approx a \) (slit width): significant diffraction
  • \( \lambda \ll a \): minimal diffraction (waves pass through mostly straight)
  • \( \lambda \gg a \): waves spread out in all directions

Single-Slit Diffraction

Light passing through a single narrow slit produces a central bright maximum with dimmer secondary maxima on either side. The minima (dark fringes) occur at:

\[ a\sin\theta = m\lambda \quad (m = \pm 1, \pm 2, \pm 3, ...) \]

where \( a \) = slit width. The central maximum is twice as wide as the secondary maxima.

Key Features

  • Narrower slit → wider diffraction pattern (more spreading)
  • Longer wavelength → wider diffraction pattern
  • Central maximum contains most of the light energy
Key Idea: Diffraction is more pronounced when the wavelength is comparable to the size of the opening. This is why sound (\( \lambda \sim 1 \) m) diffracts around corners but light (\( \lambda \sim 500 \) nm) does not noticeably diffract around doorways.
AP Exam Tip: Don't confuse single-slit diffraction minima with double-slit interference maxima. Single slit: \( a\sin\theta = m\lambda \) gives minima. Double slit: \( d\sin\theta = m\lambda \) gives maxima.

problems.question_html: If a wave's wavelength is much smaller than an opening it passes through, the amount of diffraction is:

choices.text: Minimal — the wave passes through mostly straight
Maximum — the wave spreads out completely

hints.text: Diffraction is most significant when \( \lambda \approx a \).
When \( \lambda \ll a \), diffraction is minimal — the wave goes mostly straight through.

solution_steps.text: When \( \lambda \ll a \) (wavelength much smaller than opening), diffraction is negligible. The wave passes through with minimal bending.

problems.question_html: A single slit of width \( a = 0.10 \) mm is illuminated by 500 nm light. At what angle does the first minimum occur?

hints.text: First minimum: \( a\sin\theta = \lambda \) (\( m = 1 \)).

problems.question_html: You can hear someone around a corner but can't see them. This is because:

hints.text: Diffraction is most significant when \( \lambda \) is comparable to the obstacle/opening size.
Sound waves (\( \lambda \sim 1 \) m) are comparable to doorway size → significant diffraction. Light waves (\( \lambda \sim 500 \) nm) are much smaller → negligible diffraction around corners.

solution_steps.text: Sound wavelengths (~1 m) are comparable to doorway widths, so sound diffracts around corners effectively.
Light wavelengths (~500 nm) are millions of times smaller than doorways → negligible diffraction.

problems.question_html: If the slit width is halved (made narrower), the central diffraction maximum becomes:

hints.text: The angle of the first minimum is \( \sin\theta = \lambda/a \). What happens when \( a \) decreases?
Smaller \( a \) → larger \( \theta \) → wider central maximum. Counterintuitively, a narrower slit produces a wider diffraction pattern.

solution_steps.text: \( \sin\theta = \lambda/a \). If \( a \) halves, \( \theta \) doubles → the central maximum becomes wider.
Narrower slit → more spreading → wider diffraction pattern.

problems.question_html: In single-slit diffraction, the central maximum is:

choices.text: Twice as wide as the secondary maxima
The same width as the secondary maxima
Half as wide as the secondary maxima

hints.text: The first minima occur at \( \pm \lambda/a \). How wide is the central maximum compared to the spacing between secondary maxima?
Central maximum extends from \( -\lambda/a \) to \( +\lambda/a \), width \( 2\lambda/a \). Secondary maxima are each \( \lambda/a \) wide. So the central maximum is twice as wide.

solution_steps.text: Central maximum: from first minimum at \( -\lambda/a \) to \( +\lambda/a \) → angular width \( 2\lambda/a \).
Secondary maxima: angular width \( \lambda/a \) each. Central is twice as wide.

problems.question_html: Light of wavelength 600 nm passes through a 0.15 mm slit. What is the angle to the second minimum?

hints.text: Second minimum: \( a\sin\theta = 2\lambda \).

problems.question_html: How does the single-slit diffraction pattern change if the wavelength is increased while keeping the slit width constant?

hints.text: The angle of the minima depends on \( \lambda/a \).
Larger \( \lambda \) → larger \( \sin\theta = m\lambda/a \) → wider pattern. All maxima and minima spread further apart.

solution_steps.text: \( \sin\theta = m\lambda/a \). Increasing \( \lambda \) increases \( \theta \) for each minimum.
The entire diffraction pattern gets wider (spreads out more).

problems.question_html: A single slit produces a diffraction pattern on a screen 2.0 m away. The slit width is 0.10 mm and the light wavelength is 500 nm. How wide is the central maximum on the screen, in cm? (Use small angle: \( y \approx L\tan\theta \approx L\sin\theta \).)
problems.sample_answer: First minimum at sinθ = λ/a = (500e-9)/(0.10e-3) = 5.0e-3. For small angles, y₁ = Lsinθ = (2.0)(5.0e-3) = 0.010 m = 1.0 cm. The central maximum extends from -y₁ to +y₁, so its total width is 2y₁ = 2.0 cm.
rubric: Correctly finds angle of first minimum: sinθ = λ/a = 5.0 × 10⁻³ (1 point)
Correctly finds position on screen: y = Lsinθ = 0.010 m = 1.0 cm (1 point)
States total width = 2y = 2.0 cm (the central max extends on both sides) (1 point)

hints.text: First minimum: \( \sin\theta = \lambda/a \). Position on screen: \( y = L\sin\theta \). Central max width = \( 2y \).

problems.correct_answer: First minimum at sinθ = λ/a = (500e-9)/(0.10e-3) = 5.0e-3. For small angles, y₁ = Lsinθ = (2.0)(5.0e-3) = 0.010 m = 1.0 cm. The central maximum extends from -y₁ to +y₁, so its total width is 2y₁ = 2.0 cm.

concepts.title: Double-Slit Interference and Diffraction Gratings
concepts.content_html:
Double-Slit Interference and Diffraction Gratings

In 1801, Thomas Young demonstrated that light is a wave by shining it through two narrow slits and observing an interference pattern of bright and dark fringes on a screen.

Double-Slit Interference

Two slits separated by distance \( d \) produce bright fringes (constructive interference) at angles where:

\[ d\sin\theta = m\lambda \quad (m = 0, \pm 1, \pm 2, ...) \]

Dark fringes (destructive interference) occur at:

\[ d\sin\theta = (m + \tfrac{1}{2})\lambda \]

On a screen at distance \( L \), the position of the \( m \)th bright fringe is:

\[ y_m = \frac{m\lambda L}{d} \]

Fringe Spacing

The distance between consecutive bright fringes:

\[ \Delta y = \frac{\lambda L}{d} \]

Larger \( \lambda \) or \( L \) → wider spacing. Larger \( d \) → narrower spacing.

Diffraction Gratings

A diffraction grating has many slits (hundreds or thousands per mm), producing the same maxima condition: \( d\sin\theta = m\lambda \), but with much sharper and brighter peaks. Gratings are used to precisely measure wavelengths (spectroscopy).

The grating spacing \( d = 1/N \) where \( N \) is the number of lines per meter.

Key Idea: Double slit: \( d\sin\theta = m\lambda \) gives bright fringes (maxima). Compare with single slit: \( a\sin\theta = m\lambda \) gives dark fringes (minima). Don't confuse them!
AP Exam Tip: Fringe spacing \( \Delta y = \lambda L/d \). Increasing wavelength (red vs. blue), increasing screen distance, or decreasing slit separation all make fringes wider apart. The exam tests all three variations.

problems.question_html: In Young's double-slit experiment, the condition for a bright fringe (constructive interference) is:

hints.text: Constructive interference requires the path difference to be a whole number of wavelengths.
Bright fringes: \( d\sin\theta = m\lambda \) (\( m = 0, \pm 1, \pm 2, ... \)). Dark fringes: \( d\sin\theta = (m + \frac{1}{2})\lambda \).

solution_steps.text: Constructive (bright): \( d\sin\theta = m\lambda \). Path difference = integer multiple of \( \lambda \).

problems.question_html: Two slits separated by 0.50 mm are illuminated by 600 nm light. A screen is 1.5 m away. What is the distance between adjacent bright fringes on the screen?

hints.text: Fringe spacing: \( \Delta y = \lambda L/d \).

problems.question_html: A diffraction grating has 500 lines per mm. What is the slit spacing \( d \) in micrometers (μm)?

hints.text: \( d = 1/N \) where \( N \) is lines per unit length.

problems.question_html: If the slit separation is doubled in a double-slit experiment (everything else stays the same), the fringe spacing:

hints.text: \( \Delta y = \lambda L/d \). What happens when \( d \) doubles?
\( \Delta y \propto 1/d \). If \( d \) doubles, \( \Delta y \) halves. Fringes get closer together.

solution_steps.text: \( \Delta y = \lambda L/d \). Doubling \( d \) → \( \Delta y \) halves. Fringes become half as far apart.

problems.question_html: How does a diffraction grating produce sharper maxima than a double slit, even though the same equation \( d\sin\theta = m\lambda \) applies?

choices.text: More slits means more waves must be in phase, creating narrower peaks
The grating has smaller slit spacing

hints.text: What happens when many waves (not just two) must simultaneously be in phase?

With N slits, all N waves must be in phase for a maximum. Even a slight deviation from the correct angle causes destructive interference among the many waves. More slits → sharper (narrower, brighter) peaks.

solution_steps.text: A grating has many slits (N >> 2). All N waves must be in phase for constructive interference.
At angles slightly off from \( d\sin\theta = m\lambda \), the N waves destructively interfere → very narrow, sharp peaks.

problems.question_html: In a double-slit experiment with 500 nm light, the 3rd-order bright fringe occurs at 0.15° from the central maximum. What is the slit separation?

hints.text: \( d\sin\theta = m\lambda \). Solve for \( d \) with \( m = 3 \).

problems.question_html: A diffraction grating with 600 lines/mm is used to observe 550 nm light. At what angle does the first-order maximum occur?

hints.text: \( d = 1/600 \) mm. Use \( d\sin\theta = m\lambda \) with \( m = 1 \).

problems.question_html: In the double-slit experiment above (\( d = 0.50 \) mm, \( \lambda = 600 \) nm, \( L = 1.5 \) m), at what distance from the central maximum on the screen is the second bright fringe, in mm?

hints.text: \( y_m = m\lambda L/d \) with \( m = 2 \).

problems.question_html: White light (400–700 nm) passes through a double slit. The first-order fringes of red (700 nm) and violet (400 nm) light are at different positions. Which color's fringe is farther from the center, and by what factor?
problems.sample_answer: y_m = mλL/d. For the same m, d, and L, the position is proportional to λ. Red (700 nm) has a longer wavelength than violet (400 nm), so red fringes are farther from the center. Ratio: y_red/y_violet = 700/400 = 1.75. Red fringes are 1.75 times farther from the center than violet fringes.
rubric: Identifies that fringe position is proportional to wavelength (y ∝ λ) (1 point)
Correctly states red is farther from center because it has longer wavelength (1 point)
Calculates ratio y_red/y_violet = 700/400 = 1.75 (1 point)

hints.text: \( y_m \propto \lambda \). Which color has the longer wavelength?
Red (700 nm) is farther. Ratio: 700/400 = 1.75.

solution_steps.text: \( y_m = m\lambda L/d \). For constant \( m, L, d \): \( y \propto \lambda \).
Red (\( \lambda = 700 \) nm) → farther from center. Violet (\( \lambda = 400 \) nm) → closer.
\( y_{\text{red}}/y_{\text{violet}} = 700/400 = 1.75 \). Red fringes are 1.75× farther from the center.

problems.correct_answer: y_m = mλL/d. For the same m, d, and L, the position is proportional to λ. Red (700 nm) has a longer wavelength than violet (400 nm), so red fringes are farther from the center. Ratio: y_red/y_violet = 700/400 = 1.75. Red fringes are 1.75 times farther from the center than violet fringes.

concepts.title: Thin-Film Interference
concepts.content_html:
Thin-Film Interference

The colorful swirls on a soap bubble and the rainbow sheen on an oil slick are caused by thin-film interference — light reflecting off the top and bottom surfaces of a thin transparent film interferes with itself.

How It Works

Light hits a thin film (thickness \( t \), index \( n \)). Some reflects off the top surface; some enters the film, reflects off the bottom surface, and exits. These two reflected rays interfere.

Phase Changes on Reflection

Critical rule: when light reflects off a surface with a higher index of refraction, it undergoes a 180° phase change (equivalent to \( \lambda/2 \) shift). When it reflects off a surface with a lower \( n \), there is no phase change.

Path Difference

The ray inside the film travels an extra path of \( 2t \) (down and back up). The wavelength inside the film is \( \lambda_n = \lambda/n \).

Conditions for Interference

Count the total phase shifts from reflection, then compare with the path difference:

  • 0 or 2 phase changes (same effect): constructive when \( 2t = m\lambda_n \); destructive when \( 2t = (m + \frac{1}{2})\lambda_n \)
  • 1 phase change: constructive when \( 2t = (m + \frac{1}{2})\lambda_n \); destructive when \( 2t = m\lambda_n \)

where \( \lambda_n = \lambda/n_{\text{film}} \) and \( m = 0, 1, 2, ... \)

Key Idea: Always count the phase changes first! Reflection from a higher-\( n \) surface → 180° phase change. Then determine whether constructive or destructive interference occurs.
AP Exam Tip: The minimum non-zero thickness for constructive interference with 1 phase change is \( t = \lambda/(4n) \) (set \( m = 0 \) in \( 2t = \frac{1}{2}\lambda_n \)). This is a very common AP question.

problems.question_html: When light reflects off a surface with a higher index of refraction, it undergoes a phase change of:

hints.text: This is analogous to a wave pulse reflecting off a fixed end (denser medium).
Reflection from a higher-\( n \) surface → 180° phase change (like a fixed-end reflection). Reflection from a lower-\( n \) surface → 0° phase change (like a free-end reflection).

solution_steps.text: Higher \( n \) → 180° phase change on reflection. Lower \( n \) → no phase change. Analogous to fixed vs. free end of a string.

problems.question_html: A soap film (\( n = 1.33 \)) in air appears bright (constructive reflection) for 532 nm light. If there is one net phase change, what is the minimum thickness of the film?

hints.text: With 1 phase change, constructive interference: \( 2t = (m + \frac{1}{2})\lambda_n \). Minimum when \( m = 0 \).

solution_steps.text: With 1 phase change, constructive: \( 2t = (m + \frac{1}{2})\lambda_n \). Minimum at \( m = 0 \): \( 2t = \lambda_n/2 \).

problems.question_html: A thin oil film (\( n = 1.45 \)) floats on water (\( n = 1.33 \)). Light reflects from both the top surface (air→oil) and bottom surface (oil→water). How many 180° phase changes occur?

hints.text: Check each reflection: does the light go to a higher or lower \( n \)?
Top: air (1.00) → oil (1.45): higher \( n \) → 180° phase change ✓. Bottom: oil (1.45) → water (1.33): lower \( n \) → no phase change ✗. Total: 1 phase change.

solution_steps.text: Top surface: air (\( n = 1.00 \)) → oil (\( n = 1.45 \)): higher \( n \) → 180° phase change.
Bottom surface: oil (\( n = 1.45 \)) → water (\( n = 1.33 \)): lower \( n \) → no phase change.

problems.question_html: Why do soap bubbles show rainbow colors?
problems.correct_answer: different thicknesses constructively reflect different wavelengths

hints.text: The condition for constructive interference depends on both thickness and wavelength.

The soap film has varying thickness. At each point, a different wavelength satisfies the constructive interference condition \( 2t = (m + \frac{1}{2})\lambda_n \), so different colors appear at different locations.

solution_steps.text: The soap film varies in thickness across its surface.
At each thickness, a specific wavelength satisfies constructive interference and is strongly reflected. Different thicknesses → different colors → rainbow appearance.

problems.question_html: A glass plate (\( n = 1.50 \)) has a thin coating (\( n = 1.25 \)) in air. How many phase changes occur for reflected light?

hints.text: Check each reflection surface: is light going to higher or lower \( n \)?
Top: air (1.00) → coating (1.25): higher \( n \) → 180°. Bottom: coating (1.25) → glass (1.50): higher \( n \) → 180°. Total: 2 phase changes.

solution_steps.text: Air → coating: 1.00 < 1.25 → phase change. Coating → glass: 1.25 < 1.50 → phase change.
Total: 2 phase changes (net zero effective shift).

problems.question_html: Why does an anti-reflective coating need both the correct thickness AND the correct index of refraction to work effectively?

choices.text: The thickness controls the path difference and the index determines the number of phase changes
Only the thickness matters; the index is irrelevant
Only the index matters; the thickness is irrelevant
The coating absorbs light, and both properties affect absorption

hints.text: Anti-reflective coatings work by destructive interference of reflected rays. What two things determine whether interference is constructive or destructive?

The index determines (1) the number of phase changes at each surface and (2) the wavelength inside the film (\( \lambda_n = \lambda/n \)). The thickness determines the path difference (\( 2t \)). Both must be right for destructive interference of reflected light.

solution_steps.text: The coating's index determines phase changes on reflection and the effective wavelength inside the film.
The thickness controls the path difference between the two reflected rays.
Both must be chosen correctly to achieve destructive interference (cancellation) of reflected light.

problems.question_html: An anti-reflective coating (\( n = 1.38 \)) is applied to glass (\( n = 1.50 \)). For 550 nm light, what is the minimum coating thickness for destructive interference in the reflected light?

hints.text: Count phase changes: air→coating (higher n → 180°) and coating→glass (higher n → 180°). That's 2 phase changes (net 0 effect).
With 0 or 2 phase changes, destructive: \( 2t = (m + \frac{1}{2})\lambda_n \). \( \lambda_n = 550/1.38 = 399 \) nm. Min at \( m = 0 \): \( t = \lambda_n/4 = 399/4 \approx 99.6 \) nm.

solution_steps.text: Phase changes: air (1.00) → coating (1.38): ↑n, 180°. Coating (1.38) → glass (1.50): ↑n, 180°. Total: 2 changes (net zero effect).
With 0 net phase change, destructive when \( 2t = (m + \frac{1}{2})\lambda_n \). \( \lambda_n = 550/1.38 = 399 \) nm.

problems.question_html: A soap film (\( n = 1.33 \)) in air has a thickness of 300 nm. What visible wavelength (400–700 nm) is most strongly reflected? (1 phase change occurs.)

hints.text: With 1 phase change, constructive: \( 2t = (m + \frac{1}{2})\lambda_n \). \( \lambda_n = \lambda/n \). Find \( \lambda \) in the visible range.

solution_steps.text: \( m = 0 \): \( \lambda = 1596 \) nm (infrared — not visible). \( m = 1 \): \( \lambda = 798/1.5 = 532 \) nm (green — visible ✓).
\( m = 2 \): \( \lambda = 798/2.5 = 319 \) nm (UV — not visible). Answer: 532 nm.

problems.question_html: An oil film (\( n = 1.45 \)) on water (\( n = 1.33 \)) is illuminated by white light. The film appears blue (480 nm strongly reflected). If there is 1 phase change, determine two possible thicknesses of the oil film.
problems.sample_answer: With 1 phase change, constructive: 2t = (m + 1/2)λₙ where λₙ = 480/1.45 = 331 nm. For m = 0: 2t = (0.5)(331) = 166 nm → t = 83 nm. For m = 1: 2t = (1.5)(331) = 497 nm → t = 248 nm.
rubric: Correctly calculates λₙ = λ/n = 480/1.45 = 331 nm (1 point)
Uses correct constructive condition for 1 phase change: 2t = (m + 1/2)λₙ (1 point)
Correctly finds two thicknesses: t = 83 nm (m=0) and t = 248 nm (m=1) (1 point)

hints.text: \( \lambda_n = \lambda/n_{\text{film}} \). With 1 phase change, constructive: \( 2t = (m + \frac{1}{2})\lambda_n \).

problems.correct_answer: With 1 phase change, constructive: 2t = (m + 1/2)λₙ where λₙ = 480/1.45 = 331 nm. For m = 0: 2t = (0.5)(331) = 166 nm → t = 83 nm. For m = 1: 2t = (1.5)(331) = 497 nm → t = 248 nm.

concepts.title: Quantum Theory and Wave-Particle Duality
concepts.content_html:
Quantum Theory and Wave-Particle Duality

By the early 20th century, experiments showed that light sometimes acts like a wave (interference, diffraction) and sometimes like a particle (photoelectric effect). Similarly, particles like electrons can behave like waves. This is wave-particle duality.

Light as Particles: Photons

Light comes in discrete packets of energy called photons. Each photon carries energy:

\[ E = hf = \frac{hc}{\lambda} \]

where \( h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \) J·s is Planck's constant. Photon momentum:

\[ p = \frac{h}{\lambda} = \frac{E}{c} \]

Matter as Waves: de Broglie Wavelength

Any moving particle has an associated wavelength:

\[ \lambda = \frac{h}{p} = \frac{h}{mv} \]

For macroscopic objects, \( \lambda \) is unimaginably small. For electrons, \( \lambda \) is comparable to atomic dimensions — which is why electron diffraction is observable.

Evidence for Duality

  • Light as wave: double-slit interference, diffraction
  • Light as particle: photoelectric effect, Compton scattering
  • Electrons as wave: electron diffraction through crystals
  • Electrons as particle: detected as individual hits on a screen
Key Idea: Wave-particle duality applies to both light and matter. The de Broglie wavelength connects particle momentum to wave behavior: \( \lambda = h/p \).
AP Exam Tip: The de Broglie wavelength \( \lambda = h/(mv) \) is inversely proportional to both mass and speed. Heavier or faster particles have shorter wavelengths.

problems.question_html: What is the energy of a photon of green light (\( \lambda = 500 \) nm)? (\( h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \) J·s, \( c = 3.0 \times 10^8 \) m/s)

hints.text: Use \( E = hc/\lambda \).

problems.question_html: What is the de Broglie wavelength of an electron (\( m = 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \) kg) moving at \( 1.0 \times 10^6 \) m/s?

hints.text: \( \lambda = h/(mv) \).

problems.question_html: If an electron's speed doubles, its de Broglie wavelength:

hints.text: \( \lambda = h/(mv) \). How does \( \lambda \) depend on \( v \)?
\( \lambda \propto 1/v \). If \( v \) doubles, \( \lambda \) halves.

solution_steps.text: \( \lambda = h/(mv) \propto 1/v \). Doubling speed halves the wavelength.

problems.question_html: Which experiment provides evidence that light behaves as particles?

hints.text: This experiment showed that light ejects electrons from metals, and the energy depends on frequency, not intensity.
The photoelectric effect (explained by Einstein in 1905) showed light behaves as particles (photons).

solution_steps.text: The photoelectric effect demonstrates light's particle nature. Photon energy \( E = hf \) determines whether electrons are ejected, not light intensity.

problems.question_html: A neutron (\( m = 1.67 \times 10^{-27} \) kg) has a de Broglie wavelength of 0.10 nm. What is its speed?

hints.text: Rearrange \( \lambda = h/(mv) \) to \( v = h/(m\lambda) \).

problems.question_html: Compare the de Broglie wavelength of a proton and an electron moving at the same speed. Which has the longer wavelength?

hints.text: \( \lambda = h/(mv) \). Same \( v \) → \( \lambda \propto 1/m \).
The electron has smaller mass → larger \( \lambda \). Since \( m_p \approx 1836 m_e \), the electron's wavelength is about 1836× longer.

solution_steps.text: \( \lambda \propto 1/m \) (at same speed). Electron is lighter → longer wavelength.

problems.question_html: What is the momentum of a photon with wavelength 400 nm? (\( h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \) J·s)

hints.text: Photon momentum: \( p = h/\lambda \).

problems.question_html: Explain how the double-slit experiment with single electrons demonstrates wave-particle duality.
problems.sample_answer: When single electrons are sent one at a time through a double slit, each electron hits the detector screen at a single point (particle behavior). However, after many electrons have been detected, their positions form an interference pattern identical to the pattern produced by waves passing through two slits. This means each individual electron somehow interferes with itself — passing through both slits as a probability wave, but arriving as a discrete particle. This is the essence of wave-particle duality.
rubric: States that individual electrons arrive as localized particles (single detection points) (1 point)
States that the cumulative pattern of many electrons shows wave-like interference fringes (1 point)
Connects this to wave-particle duality: each electron exhibits both wave and particle behavior (1 point)

hints.text: What does each electron look like when it hits the screen? What does the pattern of many electrons look like?
Individual electron → single dot (particle). Many electrons → interference pattern (wave). The electron passes through both slits as a probability wave but arrives as a particle.

solution_steps.text: Each electron arrives at a single point on the screen → particle behavior.
After many electrons, the collective pattern shows bright and dark fringes → wave interference pattern.
Each electron passes through both slits simultaneously as a probability wave, then collapses to a point when detected. This is wave-particle duality.

problems.correct_answer: When single electrons are sent one at a time through a double slit, each electron hits the detector screen at a single point (particle behavior). However, after many electrons have been detected, their positions form an interference pattern identical to the pattern produced by waves passing through two slits. This means each individual electron somehow interferes with itself — passing through both slits as a probability wave, but arriving as a discrete particle. This is the essence of wave-particle duality.

concepts.title: The Bohr Model of Atomic Structure
concepts.content_html:
The Bohr Model of Atomic Structure

In 1913, Niels Bohr proposed that electrons orbit the nucleus in specific, quantized energy levels — they can only exist at certain discrete energies, not in between.

Bohr's Postulates

  1. Electrons orbit in specific stationary states without radiating energy
  2. Electrons can only transition between energy levels by absorbing or emitting a photon with energy \( E = hf \) equal to the energy difference between levels
  3. Allowed orbits have quantized angular momentum

Energy Levels of Hydrogen

\[ E_n = -\frac{13.6 \text{ eV}}{n^2} \quad (n = 1, 2, 3, ...) \]

  • \( n = 1 \): ground state (\( E_1 = -13.6 \) eV)
  • \( n = 2 \): first excited state (\( E_2 = -3.4 \) eV)
  • \( n = \infty \): ionization (\( E = 0 \) eV)

Negative energy means the electron is bound. The ionization energy is 13.6 eV (energy needed to remove the electron from the ground state).

Photon Energy from Transitions

\[ E_{\text{photon}} = |E_f - E_i| = hf = \frac{hc}{\lambda} \]

Electron drops to lower level → photon emitted. Electron jumps to higher level → photon absorbed.

Key Idea: Electrons can only exist at specific energy levels. Transitions between levels produce or absorb photons with energy exactly equal to the energy difference.
AP Exam Tip: The exam often gives an energy level diagram and asks which transitions produce visible light. Visible photons have energies of about 1.8 eV (red) to 3.1 eV (violet). The \( n = 2 \) to \( n = 1 \) transition (10.2 eV) is in the UV, not visible.

problems.question_html: What is the energy of a hydrogen electron in the \( n = 3 \) level?
A hydrogen electron transitions from \( n = 3 \) to \( n = 2 \). What is the energy of the emitted photon?

hints.text: Photon energy = \( |E_3 - E_2| \).

problems.question_html: What is the ionization energy of hydrogen from the ground state, in eV?

hints.text: Ionization means removing the electron to \( n = \infty \) (\( E = 0 \)).
From ground state: \( E_{\text{ion}} = 0 - (-13.6) = 13.6 \) eV.

problems.question_html: In the Bohr model, when an electron transitions to a lower energy level, what happens?

hints.text: The electron loses energy. Where does that energy go?
The energy difference is carried away as a photon: \( E_{\text{photon}} = E_i - E_f \).

solution_steps.text: Transition to a lower energy level → energy is released as a photon with \( E = hf = |E_i - E_f| \).

problems.question_html: Which hydrogen transition produces the longest wavelength in the Balmer series (transitions to \( n = 2 \))?

hints.text: Longest wavelength = smallest energy difference. Which transition has the smallest \( \Delta E \)?
\( n = 3 \to 2 \): smallest energy gap in the Balmer series → longest wavelength (656 nm, red).

solution_steps.text: Longest wavelength = lowest energy photon = smallest \( \Delta E \).
\( n = 3 \to 2 \) has the smallest gap: 1.89 eV → \( \lambda = 656 \) nm (red). This is the H-alpha line.

problems.question_html: A hydrogen atom absorbs a photon and its electron jumps from \( n = 1 \) to \( n = 4 \). What is the wavelength of the photon? (1 eV = \( 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \) J)

hints.text: Find \( \Delta E = E_4 - E_1 \), convert to joules, then use \( \lambda = hc/E \).

problems.question_html: A hydrogen atom in the \( n = 4 \) state can emit photons by transitioning to lower levels. How many different spectral lines can it produce?

hints.text: Count all possible transitions: \( 4 \to 3 \), \( 4 \to 2 \), \( 4 \to 1 \), \( 3 \to 2 \), \( 3 \to 1 \), \( 2 \to 1 \).
From \( n = 4 \): possible transitions are \( 4 \to 3, 4 \to 2, 4 \to 1, 3 \to 2, 3 \to 1, 2 \to 1 \). That's \( C(4,2) = 6 \) lines.

solution_steps.text: Number of spectral lines from level \( n \): \( n(n-1)/2 = 4(3)/2 = 6 \).

problems.question_html: A hydrogen atom is in the \( n = 2 \) state. A photon of energy 2.55 eV strikes it. Can the atom absorb this photon? Explain.
problems.sample_answer: E₂ = −3.40 eV. The next level is n = 3: E₃ = −1.51 eV. ΔE = −1.51 − (−3.40) = 1.89 eV. The next is n = 4: E₄ = −0.85 eV. ΔE = −0.85 − (−3.40) = 2.55 eV. Yes! The 2.55 eV photon exactly matches the n=2 to n=4 transition, so it can be absorbed. The electron jumps to n = 4.
rubric: Calculates energy levels E₂, E₃, E₄ correctly (1 point)
Identifies that 2.55 eV exactly matches the n=2 to n=4 transition (1 point)
Concludes that the photon can be absorbed and the electron jumps to n=4 (1 point)

hints.text: Check if 2.55 eV matches the energy difference between \( n = 2 \) and any higher level.
\( E_2 = -3.40 \) eV. \( E_4 = -0.85 \) eV. \( \Delta E = 2.55 \) eV — exact match! The photon is absorbed.

solution_steps.text: \( E_2 = -3.40 \) eV. Check transitions: \( E_3 - E_2 = 1.89 \) eV (no match). \( E_4 - E_2 = 2.55 \) eV (match!).
The 2.55 eV photon exactly matches the \( n = 2 \to n = 4 \) transition.
Yes, the photon is absorbed and the electron jumps to \( n = 4 \). (If the photon energy didn't match any transition, it would not be absorbed.)

problems.correct_answer: E₂ = −3.40 eV. The next level is n = 3: E₃ = −1.51 eV. ΔE = −1.51 − (−3.40) = 1.89 eV. The next is n = 4: E₄ = −0.85 eV. ΔE = −0.85 − (−3.40) = 2.55 eV. Yes! The 2.55 eV photon exactly matches the n=2 to n=4 transition, so it can be absorbed. The electron jumps to n = 4.

concepts.title: Emission and Absorption Spectra
concepts.content_html:
Emission and Absorption Spectra

Every element has a unique set of energy levels, producing a unique spectral fingerprint. This is how astronomers identify elements in distant stars.

Three Types of Spectra

  • Continuous spectrum: a hot, dense object (like a light bulb filament) emits all wavelengths — a smooth rainbow
  • Emission spectrum: a hot, low-density gas emits light only at specific wavelengths — bright lines on a dark background
  • Absorption spectrum: white light passing through a cool gas has specific wavelengths absorbed — dark lines on a continuous background

Kirchhoff's Laws of Spectroscopy

  1. Hot, dense object → continuous spectrum
  2. Hot, thin gas → emission line spectrum
  3. Continuous light through cool gas → absorption line spectrum

Emission = Absorption (Same Lines)

The wavelengths in an element's emission spectrum are exactly the same as in its absorption spectrum — both correspond to transitions between the same energy levels.

Key Idea: Each element produces a unique set of spectral lines. Emission and absorption spectra are complementary — same wavelengths, but bright lines vs. dark lines.
AP Exam Tip: The exam may show a spectrum and ask you to identify which transitions produced which lines. Use \( \Delta E = hf = hc/\lambda \) and the energy level diagram.

problems.question_html: A hot, low-density gas produces which type of spectrum?

hints.text: Hot gas emits light. Low density means individual atoms radiate independently.
Hot, thin gas → bright lines at specific wavelengths = emission line spectrum.

solution_steps.text: Hot, low-density gas → emission line spectrum (bright lines at wavelengths corresponding to energy level transitions).

problems.question_html: An absorption spectrum shows:

choices.text: Dark lines on a continuous (rainbow) background
Bright lines on a dark background

hints.text: Light from a continuous source passes through cool gas. The gas absorbs specific wavelengths.
Absorption spectrum = continuous background with dark lines at the same wavelengths that the gas would emit.

solution_steps.text: Absorption spectrum: continuous light minus specific wavelengths absorbed by the gas → dark lines on rainbow background.

problems.question_html: The emission spectrum lines of an element appear at the same wavelengths as its:

hints.text: Both emission and absorption involve transitions between the same energy levels.
Emission and absorption spectra have the same wavelengths — they are complementary. Same transitions, but emission = bright lines, absorption = dark lines.

solution_steps.text: An element's emission and absorption spectra have the same wavelengths, because both correspond to the same energy level transitions.

problems.question_html: How do astronomers determine the chemical composition of a distant star?

hints.text: Starlight passes through the star's outer atmosphere before reaching us.
Each element absorbs specific wavelengths. By matching the dark lines in a star's absorption spectrum to known element spectra, astronomers identify the elements present.

solution_steps.text: Stars produce a continuous spectrum, modified by absorption in their atmospheres. The dark absorption lines reveal which elements are present — each element has a unique spectral fingerprint.

problems.question_html: Two gas samples produce the same spectral lines but at different intensities. This indicates:

choices.text: They contain the same element but may differ in temperature or density
One is hotter than the other and therefore a different element

hints.text: Spectral line wavelengths identify the element. What determines line intensity?
Same wavelengths = same element. Intensity depends on the number of atoms in each energy state, which depends on temperature and density.

solution_steps.text: Same spectral lines = same element (wavelengths are determined by energy levels).
Different intensities indicate different temperatures, densities, or amounts of the gas.

problems.question_html: Why can't hydrogen gas at room temperature produce emission lines in the visible range?

choices.text: At room temperature, virtually all electrons are in the ground state and can't emit photons
Hydrogen doesn't have visible emission lines
Room temperature light is too bright

hints.text: Emission requires electrons in excited states. What determines whether atoms are in excited states?
At room temperature, thermal energy (\( \sim 0.025 \) eV) is far too low to excite hydrogen (10.2 eV for \( n = 1 \to 2 \)). All electrons stay in the ground state — no transitions down, no emission.

solution_steps.text: At room temperature, \( kT \approx 0.025 \) eV. The first excited state of hydrogen requires 10.2 eV.
Virtually no atoms are excited → no downward transitions → no emission spectrum.

concepts.title: Blackbody Radiation
concepts.content_html:
Blackbody Radiation

Every object above absolute zero emits electromagnetic radiation. A blackbody is an idealized object that absorbs all incoming radiation and emits a characteristic spectrum that depends only on its temperature.

Key Features of Blackbody Spectra

  • The spectrum is a smooth, continuous curve
  • Higher temperature → more total energy emitted (curve is taller) AND peak shifts to shorter wavelength (bluer)
  • All objects glow: red hot (~800 K), white hot (~6000 K), blue hot (~10000 K)

Wien's Displacement Law

The peak wavelength is inversely proportional to temperature:

\[ \lambda_{\max} = \frac{2.90 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m·K}}{T} \]

Stefan-Boltzmann Law

Total power radiated per unit area:

\[ P/A = \sigma T^4 \]

where \( \sigma = 5.67 \times 10^{-8} \) W/(m²·K⁴). Double the temperature → 16× the power.

The Ultraviolet Catastrophe and Planck

Classical physics predicted infinite energy at short wavelengths — the "ultraviolet catastrophe." Max Planck resolved this in 1900 by proposing that energy is emitted in discrete packets (quanta): \( E = nhf \). This was the birth of quantum theory.

Key Idea: Hotter objects emit more radiation (\( \propto T^4 \)) and at shorter peak wavelengths. This is why hot stars appear blue and cool stars appear red.
AP Exam Tip: Wien's law: \( \lambda_{\max} \propto 1/T \). Stefan-Boltzmann: \( P \propto T^4 \). Know how to use both, and remember that doubling \( T \) means 16× the radiated power.

problems.question_html: The Sun's surface temperature is about 5800 K. What is the peak wavelength of its radiation? (\( b = 2.90 \times 10^{-3} \) m·K)

hints.text: Use Wien's law: \( \lambda_{\max} = b/T \).
\( \lambda_{\max} = (2.90 \times 10^{-3})/5800 = 5.0 \times 10^{-7} \) m = 500 nm (green, in the visible range).

solution_steps.text: This is why sunlight appears white — it peaks in the middle of the visible spectrum.

problems.question_html: If a star's temperature doubles from 3000 K to 6000 K, by what factor does its radiated power per unit area increase?

hints.text: Stefan-Boltzmann: \( P/A \propto T^4 \).
If \( T \) doubles: \( (2T)^4 = 16T^4 \). Power per unit area increases by a factor of 16.

solution_steps.text: \( P/A \propto T^4 \). Doubling \( T \): \( 2^4 = 16 \). Power increases by a factor of 16.

problems.question_html: A red star has a lower surface temperature than a blue star. According to Wien's law, the red star's peak wavelength is ______ than the blue star's.

hints.text: \( \lambda_{\max} = b/T \). Lower \( T \) means what for \( \lambda \)?
Lower temperature → longer peak wavelength. Red light has longer wavelength than blue light.

solution_steps.text: \( \lambda_{\max} \propto 1/T \). Lower \( T \) → longer \( \lambda_{\max} \). Red stars are cooler with longer peak wavelengths.

problems.question_html: Planck resolved the ultraviolet catastrophe by proposing that energy is emitted in discrete packets called:

hints.text: The word shares its root with "quantum theory."
Planck proposed energy is emitted in discrete quanta: \( E = nhf \). This launched quantum theory.

solution_steps.text: Planck proposed that electromagnetic energy is quantized — emitted in discrete packets called quanta (singular: quantum), with \( E = hf \).

problems.question_html: A hot object at 1500 K has a peak wavelength of about 1.93 μm (infrared). If heated to 6000 K, what is its new peak wavelength?

hints.text: \( \lambda_{\max} \propto 1/T \). If \( T \) quadruples, \( \lambda \) is divided by 4.
\( T \) goes from 1500 to 6000 (×4). \( \lambda_{\max} = 1930/4 = 483 \) nm (visible blue-green light).

problems.question_html: Star A has temperature 4000 K and Star B has temperature 8000 K. Both have the same radius. What is the ratio of Star B's luminosity to Star A's?

hints.text: Luminosity \( L = \sigma T^4 \times 4\pi R^2 \). Same radius → \( L \propto T^4 \).

problems.question_html: The cosmic microwave background radiation has a peak wavelength of about 1.1 mm. What is its temperature?

hints.text: Use Wien's law: \( T = b/\lambda_{\max} \).
\( T = (2.90 \times 10^{-3})/(1.1 \times 10^{-3}) = 2.6 \) K. (The actual measured value is 2.725 K.)

solution_steps.text: This is the temperature of the cosmic microwave background — the afterglow of the Big Bang.

problems.question_html: Explain why classical physics fails to predict the blackbody spectrum (the "ultraviolet catastrophe") and how Planck's quantum hypothesis resolved it.
problems.sample_answer: Classical physics (the Rayleigh-Jeans law) treats electromagnetic oscillators as having any continuous energy. This predicts that the intensity increases without bound at short wavelengths (high frequencies), giving infinite total energy — the 'ultraviolet catastrophe.' Planck proposed that oscillators can only have energies in discrete multiples of hf (E = nhf). At high frequencies, hf is large, so few oscillators are excited, and the intensity drops to zero. This quantization correctly predicts the observed blackbody spectrum.
rubric: Describes the ultraviolet catastrophe: classical prediction of infinite intensity at short wavelengths (1 point)
States Planck's hypothesis: energy quantized as E = nhf (1 point)
Explains why quantization resolves the problem: high-frequency modes are suppressed because hf is too large (1 point)

hints.text: What does classical physics predict about the energy at high frequencies? What does quantization change?
Classical: energy at any frequency → infinite at high \( f \). Planck: \( E = nhf \) → high-\( f \) modes need too much energy to excite → intensity drops. Spectrum matches observation.

solution_steps.text: Classical physics: intensity \( \propto f^2 \) at all frequencies → diverges at high frequencies (ultraviolet catastrophe).
Planck's fix: energy is quantized as \( E = nhf \). At high frequencies, \( hf \) is very large.
Very few oscillators have enough energy to be excited at high \( f \), so intensity drops to zero — matching the observed spectrum.

problems.correct_answer: Classical physics (the Rayleigh-Jeans law) treats electromagnetic oscillators as having any continuous energy. This predicts that the intensity increases without bound at short wavelengths (high frequencies), giving infinite total energy — the 'ultraviolet catastrophe.' Planck proposed that oscillators can only have energies in discrete multiples of hf (E = nhf). At high frequencies, hf is large, so few oscillators are excited, and the intensity drops to zero. This quantization correctly predicts the observed blackbody spectrum.

concepts.title: The Photoelectric Effect
concepts.content_html:
The Photoelectric Effect

When light shines on a metal surface, electrons can be ejected — but only if the light's frequency is high enough. This is the photoelectric effect, explained by Einstein in 1905 using the concept of photons.

Key Observations

  • Below a threshold frequency \( f_0 \), no electrons are ejected — regardless of intensity
  • Above \( f_0 \), electrons are ejected immediately, even at very low intensity
  • Increasing intensity increases the number of ejected electrons (current), not their energy
  • Increasing frequency increases the maximum kinetic energy of ejected electrons

Einstein's Equation

\[ K_{\max} = hf - \phi \]

where:

  • \( K_{\max} \) = maximum kinetic energy of ejected electrons
  • \( hf \) = energy of the incident photon
  • \( \phi = hf_0 \) = work function (minimum energy to free an electron)

Stopping Potential

The stopping potential \( V_0 \) is the voltage needed to stop the most energetic electrons:

\[ eV_0 = K_{\max} = hf - \phi \]

Key Idea: The photoelectric effect proved that light energy comes in discrete photons. One photon ejects one electron. Below the threshold frequency, no single photon has enough energy to free an electron, no matter how many photons hit the surface.
AP Exam Tip: The graph of \( K_{\max} \) vs. \( f \) is a straight line with slope \( h \) and x-intercept \( f_0 \). The work function = \( hf_0 \). The exam often gives this graph and asks you to extract \( h \) or \( \phi \).

problems.question_html: A metal has a work function of 2.0 eV. What is the threshold frequency? (\( h = 4.14 \times 10^{-15} \) eV·s)

hints.text: At threshold: \( \phi = hf_0 \), so \( f_0 = \phi/h \).

problems.question_html: Light of frequency \( 7.0 \times 10^{14} \) Hz strikes a metal with work function 2.0 eV. What is the maximum kinetic energy of the ejected electrons?

hints.text: \( K_{\max} = hf - \phi \).

problems.question_html: In the photoelectric effect, increasing the intensity of light above the threshold frequency increases the:

hints.text: More intensity = more photons per second. Each photon ejects one electron.
More photons → more electrons ejected → higher current. But each electron's maximum KE stays the same (determined by frequency).

solution_steps.text: Higher intensity = more photons/second = more electrons ejected = more current. Maximum KE is unchanged (depends only on frequency).

problems.question_html: If light below the threshold frequency shines on a metal, electrons are ____ ejected, regardless of the light's intensity.

hints.text: Each photon must have enough energy on its own to free an electron.
Below threshold: each photon has \( E < \phi \). No single photon can free an electron. More photons (higher intensity) doesn't help — it's energy per photon that matters.

solution_steps.text: Below threshold frequency, no electrons are ejected regardless of intensity. Each photon has insufficient energy (\( hf < \phi \)).

problems.question_html: A graph of \( K_{\max} \) vs. \( f \) for the photoelectric effect is a straight line. The slope equals:

hints.text: \( K_{\max} = hf - \phi \) is in the form \( y = mx + b \).
Slope = \( h \) (Planck's constant). y-intercept = \( -\phi \). x-intercept = \( f_0 = \phi/h \).

solution_steps.text: \( K_{\max} = hf - \phi \). This is \( y = mx + b \) with slope = \( h \) and y-intercept = \( -\phi \).

problems.question_html: Two light sources — one red (650 nm) and one violet (400 nm) — shine on a metal with \( \phi = 2.5 \) eV. Which ejects electrons? (\( hc = 1240 \) eV·nm)

hints.text: Calculate each photon's energy and compare to \( \phi \).
Red: \( E = 1240/650 = 1.91 \) eV < 2.5 eV (no ejection). Violet: \( E = 1240/400 = 3.10 \) eV > 2.5 eV (ejection!). Only violet works.

solution_steps.text: Red: \( E = 1240/650 = 1.91 \) eV < \( \phi = 2.5 \) eV → no ejection.
Violet: \( E = 1240/400 = 3.10 \) eV > \( \phi = 2.5 \) eV → electrons ejected.

problems.question_html: The stopping potential for photoelectrons is 1.5 V when light of frequency \( 8.0 \times 10^{14} \) Hz is used. What is the work function of the metal?

hints.text: \( eV_0 = hf - \phi \), so \( \phi = hf - eV_0 \).

problems.question_html: A metal has a work function of 4.5 eV. What is the maximum wavelength of light that can eject electrons? (Use \( hc = 1240 \) eV·nm.)

hints.text: At threshold: \( \phi = hc/\lambda_{\max} \), so \( \lambda_{\max} = hc/\phi \).
\( \lambda_{\max} = 1240/4.5 = 276 \) nm (ultraviolet).

problems.question_html: Light of wavelength 200 nm strikes a metal with work function 3.0 eV. Determine the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons and the stopping potential. (Use \( hc = 1240 \) eV·nm.)
problems.sample_answer: E_photon = hc/λ = 1240/200 = 6.2 eV. K_max = E_photon − φ = 6.2 − 3.0 = 3.2 eV. Stopping potential: eV₀ = K_max, so V₀ = 3.2 V.
rubric: Correctly calculates photon energy: E = 1240/200 = 6.2 eV (1 point)
Correctly finds K_max = 6.2 − 3.0 = 3.2 eV (1 point)
Correctly determines stopping potential V₀ = 3.2 V (1 point)

hints.text: Find photon energy with \( E = hc/\lambda \), then \( K_{\max} = E - \phi \), then \( V_0 = K_{\max}/e \).

problems.correct_answer: E_photon = hc/λ = 1240/200 = 6.2 eV. K_max = E_photon − φ = 6.2 − 3.0 = 3.2 eV. Stopping potential: eV₀ = K_max, so V₀ = 3.2 V.

concepts.title: Compton Scattering
concepts.content_html:
Compton Scattering

In 1923, Arthur Compton showed that X-ray photons scatter off electrons like billiard balls — the photon loses energy and the electron recoils. This was powerful evidence that photons carry momentum.

The Compton Effect

When a high-energy photon (usually X-ray or gamma) collides with a free electron:

  • The photon scatters at some angle \( \theta \) with a longer wavelength (lower energy)
  • The electron recoils, carrying away kinetic energy
  • Energy and momentum are conserved (like a particle collision)

Compton Wavelength Shift

\[ \Delta\lambda = \lambda' - \lambda = \frac{h}{m_e c}(1 - \cos\theta) \]

where \( h/(m_e c) = 2.43 \times 10^{-12} \) m = 0.00243 nm is the Compton wavelength of the electron.

  • \( \theta = 0° \): no shift (photon passes straight through)
  • \( \theta = 90° \): \( \Delta\lambda = h/(m_e c) = 0.00243 \) nm
  • \( \theta = 180° \): maximum shift \( \Delta\lambda = 2h/(m_e c) = 0.00486 \) nm (head-on backscatter)

Significance

Compton scattering proved that photons have momentum (\( p = h/\lambda \)) and interact with matter like particles. This confirmed the particle nature of light beyond the photoelectric effect.

Key Idea: Compton scattering treats the photon as a particle with momentum \( p = h/\lambda \). The scattered photon has longer wavelength (less energy) — the energy goes to the electron.
AP Exam Tip: The wavelength shift depends only on the scattering angle, not on the initial wavelength. The maximum shift (\( 2h/m_ec \)) occurs at 180° (backscatter).

problems.question_html: In Compton scattering, the scattered photon has a ______ wavelength than the incident photon.

choices.text: It depends on the electron's mass

hints.text: The photon loses energy to the recoiling electron. What happens to wavelength when energy decreases?
Lower energy → lower frequency → longer wavelength. \( \lambda' > \lambda \).

solution_steps.text: The photon transfers some energy to the electron → photon energy decreases → wavelength increases (gets longer).

problems.question_html: An X-ray photon scatters at 90° off a free electron. What is the wavelength shift? (\( h/(m_e c) = 0.00243 \) nm)

hints.text: \( \Delta\lambda = \frac{h}{m_e c}(1 - \cos\theta) \). At 90°, \( \cos 90° = 0 \).

problems.question_html: Compton scattering provides evidence that photons have:

hints.text: The photon-electron collision is analyzed using conservation of energy AND conservation of ___.
Compton scattering proves photons carry momentum: \( p = h/\lambda \). The collision conserves both energy and momentum.

solution_steps.text: Compton scattering demonstrates that photons have momentum (\( p = h/\lambda = E/c \)). The scattering is analyzed as a particle collision with conservation of both energy and momentum.

problems.question_html: The maximum wavelength shift in Compton scattering occurs when the photon is scattered at what angle?

hints.text: \( \Delta\lambda = \frac{h}{m_e c}(1 - \cos\theta) \). Maximum when \( 1 - \cos\theta \) is largest.
\( \cos 180° = -1 \), so \( 1 - (-1) = 2 \). Maximum shift at 180° (backscatter): \( \Delta\lambda = 2h/(m_e c) = 0.00486 \) nm.

solution_steps.text: \( \Delta\lambda \) is maximum when \( 1 - \cos\theta \) is maximum: at \( \theta = 180° \), \( \Delta\lambda = 2h/(m_e c) \).

problems.question_html: An X-ray of wavelength 0.0500 nm undergoes Compton scattering at 180°. What is the wavelength of the scattered photon?

hints.text: \( \Delta\lambda = 2h/(m_e c) = 0.00486 \) nm at 180°.

problems.question_html: Why is Compton scattering significant for X-rays but negligible for visible light?

choices.text: The wavelength shift is a fixed amount (~0.002 nm), which is a significant fraction of X-ray wavelengths but negligible for visible light wavelengths
Visible light photons don't have momentum
X-rays are particles but visible light is a wave
Compton scattering only occurs with X-rays

hints.text: The Compton shift \( \Delta\lambda \approx 0.002 \) nm is the same regardless of initial wavelength. Compare this to X-ray vs. visible wavelengths.
X-rays: \( \lambda \sim 0.05 \) nm, shift of 0.002 nm is ~4% → detectable. Visible: \( \lambda \sim 500 \) nm, shift of 0.002 nm is ~0.0004% → negligible.

solution_steps.text: The Compton shift (~0.002 nm) is independent of initial wavelength.
For X-rays (\( \lambda \sim 0.05 \) nm), this is a significant fractional change. For visible light (\( \lambda \sim 500 \) nm), it's negligible.

problems.question_html: In Compton scattering, a photon with wavelength 0.100 nm scatters at 60°. What is the scattered wavelength, in nm? (Use 4 significant figures.)
An X-ray photon of wavelength 0.0400 nm scatters off a free electron at 90°. Find the energy transferred to the electron, in eV. (\( hc = 1240 \) eV·nm)
rubric: Correctly calculates wavelength shift and scattered wavelength (1 point)
Correctly calculates initial and final photon energies (1 point)
Correctly finds energy transferred to electron ≈ 1770 eV (1 point)

hints.text: Find \( \lambda' \), then \( E_i = hc/\lambda \) and \( E_f = hc/\lambda' \). The difference goes to the electron.

concepts.title: Fission, Fusion, and Nuclear Decay
concepts.content_html:
Fission, Fusion, and Nuclear Decay

The nucleus holds protons and neutrons together with the strong nuclear force — the strongest force in nature, but it only acts over very short distances (~10⁻¹⁵ m). Nuclear reactions can release enormous amounts of energy.

Mass-Energy Equivalence

\[ E = mc^2 \]

A small amount of mass corresponds to a huge amount of energy. In nuclear reactions, the total mass of the products is slightly less than the reactants — this "missing mass" (mass defect) is converted to energy.

Useful unit: 1 atomic mass unit (u) = 931.5 MeV/c².

Binding Energy

The binding energy is the energy required to completely break apart a nucleus into its individual protons and neutrons. Higher binding energy per nucleon → more stable nucleus. Iron-56 has the highest binding energy per nucleon.

Nuclear Fission

A heavy nucleus (like U-235) splits into two lighter nuclei plus neutrons, releasing energy. This powers nuclear reactors. The products have higher binding energy per nucleon than the original → energy is released.

Nuclear Fusion

Two light nuclei (like hydrogen isotopes) combine to form a heavier nucleus, releasing even more energy per nucleon than fission. This powers the Sun. Fusion requires extremely high temperatures to overcome electrostatic repulsion.

Key Idea: Both fission (splitting heavy nuclei) and fusion (combining light nuclei) move toward iron-56 on the binding energy curve, releasing energy. Fission goes from right to center; fusion goes from left to center.
AP Exam Tip: The exam tests your understanding of the binding energy curve. Elements lighter than iron release energy by fusion. Elements heavier than iron release energy by fission. Iron is the most stable — it can't release energy by either process.

problem_sets.title: Practice: Fission, Fusion, and Nuclear Decay

problems.question_html: In nuclear fission, a heavy nucleus:

choices.text: Splits into two lighter nuclei, releasing energy
Absorbs a photon and becomes heavier

hints.text: "Fission" means splitting apart.
Fission: a heavy nucleus (e.g., U-235) splits into lighter nuclei + neutrons, releasing energy.

solution_steps.text: Fission: heavy nucleus splits into two lighter nuclei + neutrons + energy. Example: U-235 + neutron → Ba-141 + Kr-92 + 3 neutrons + energy.

problems.question_html: Nuclear fusion powers the Sun. In fusion, light nuclei:

choices.text: Combine to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy

hints.text: "Fusion" means joining together.
Fusion: light nuclei (e.g., hydrogen isotopes) combine to form a heavier nucleus, releasing enormous energy.

solution_steps.text: Fusion: light nuclei combine → heavier nucleus + energy. In the Sun: 4 protons → He-4 + 2 positrons + 2 neutrinos + energy.

problems.question_html: According to \( E = mc^2 \), how much energy (in MeV) is equivalent to 1 atomic mass unit? (1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg)

hints.text: This is a standard conversion factor in nuclear physics.
1 u = 931.5 MeV/c². So the rest energy of 1 u of mass is 931.5 MeV.

problems.question_html: Which element has the highest binding energy per nucleon (most stable nucleus)?

hints.text: It's near the middle of the periodic table.
Iron-56 (Fe-56) has the highest binding energy per nucleon (~8.8 MeV/nucleon). Elements on either side are less tightly bound.

solution_steps.text: Iron-56 has the highest binding energy per nucleon. This is why fission of heavy elements and fusion of light elements both release energy — they both move toward iron on the binding energy curve.

problems.question_html: Why does nuclear fusion require extremely high temperatures (millions of kelvins)?

choices.text: Nuclei must overcome electrostatic repulsion between positive charges
Cold nuclei are too heavy to fuse
The strong force only works at high temperature

hints.text: Both nuclei are positively charged. What force acts between them at long range?

Both nuclei are positive → electrostatic (Coulomb) repulsion. Extremely high temperatures give nuclei enough kinetic energy to overcome this barrier and get close enough for the strong force to bind them.

solution_steps.text: Nuclei are positive → Coulomb repulsion. At normal temperatures, they can't get close enough.
At millions of kelvins, kinetic energy is sufficient to overcome the Coulomb barrier, allowing the strong nuclear force (very short range) to bind the nuclei.

problems.question_html: In the fusion reaction ²H + ³H → ⁴He + n, the mass of the reactants is 5.03005 u and the mass of the products is 5.01140 u. How much energy is released, in MeV?

hints.text: Mass defect × 931.5 MeV/u = energy released.

problems.question_html: A nuclear reaction has a mass defect of 0.0050 u. How much energy is released, in MeV?

hints.text: \( E = \Delta m \times 931.5 \) MeV.

problems.question_html: Using the binding energy per nucleon curve, explain why fission of uranium releases energy but fission of iron does not.
problems.sample_answer: Uranium (A ≈ 235) sits on the right side of the binding energy curve, where binding energy per nucleon is about 7.6 MeV/nucleon. When uranium undergoes fission, the products (A ≈ 90-140) have higher binding energy per nucleon (~8.5 MeV/nucleon). The increase in binding energy is released as kinetic energy. Iron (A ≈ 56) is at the peak of the curve (~8.8 MeV/nucleon). Its fission products would have lower binding energy per nucleon, meaning energy would need to be added, not released. Therefore iron cannot release energy by fission (or fusion).
rubric: Correctly identifies uranium's position on the curve and its lower binding energy per nucleon (1 point)
Explains that fission products have higher binding energy per nucleon → energy released (1 point)
Explains that iron is at the peak → fission products have lower binding energy → no energy release (1 point)

hints.text: Energy is released when products have higher binding energy per nucleon than reactants. Where is iron vs. uranium on the curve?
Uranium: low BE/nucleon → fission products have higher BE/nucleon → energy released. Iron: at the peak → any change gives lower BE/nucleon → no energy released.

solution_steps.text: Uranium (A ≈ 235): BE/nucleon ≈ 7.6 MeV. Fission products (A ≈ 90–140): BE/nucleon ≈ 8.5 MeV. Higher → energy released.
Iron (A ≈ 56): at the peak, BE/nucleon ≈ 8.8 MeV. Any products have lower BE/nucleon → energy must be added, not released.
Iron is the most stable nucleus — neither fission nor fusion releases energy from it.

concepts.title: Types of Radioactive Decay
concepts.content_html:
Types of Radioactive Decay

Unstable nuclei spontaneously transform by emitting particles or energy. This is radioactive decay. There are three main types.

Alpha Decay (α)

The nucleus emits an alpha particle (⁴₂He — 2 protons + 2 neutrons).

  • Atomic number decreases by 2, mass number decreases by 4
  • \( ^A_Z X \to ^{A-4}_{Z-2} Y + ^4_2 \text{He} \)
  • Least penetrating (stopped by paper or skin)
  • Most ionizing

Beta Decay (β⁻)

A neutron converts to a proton, emitting an electron (β⁻ particle) and an antineutrino.

  • Atomic number increases by 1, mass number unchanged
  • \( ^A_Z X \to ^A_{Z+1} Y + e^- + \bar{\nu}_e \)
  • Moderately penetrating (stopped by aluminum foil)

Gamma Decay (γ)

The nucleus releases excess energy as a high-energy photon. No change in atomic number or mass number.

  • Often follows alpha or beta decay
  • Most penetrating (requires thick lead or concrete)
  • Least ionizing

Half-Life

The half-life \( t_{1/2} \) is the time for half of a radioactive sample to decay:

\[ N = N_0 \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{t/t_{1/2}} \]

Key Idea: In alpha decay, the nucleus loses 2 protons and 2 neutrons. In beta decay, a neutron becomes a proton. In gamma decay, no particles change — just energy is released.
AP Exam Tip: Conservation of mass number and atomic number applies to all nuclear equations. Always verify that the sum of mass numbers and the sum of atomic numbers are equal on both sides of a nuclear equation.

problems.question_html: In alpha decay, the mass number of the daughter nucleus decreases by:

hints.text: An alpha particle is ⁴₂He. How many nucleons does it carry away?
Alpha particle = 4 nucleons (2p + 2n). Mass number decreases by 4, atomic number by 2.

solution_steps.text: Alpha decay: \( ^A_Z X \to ^{A-4}_{Z-2} Y + ^4_2 \text{He} \). Mass number decreases by 4.

problems.question_html: In beta-minus (β⁻) decay, what happens to the atomic number?

hints.text: A neutron becomes a proton. What does that do to the number of protons?
n → p + e⁻ + antineutrino. One more proton → atomic number increases by 1. Mass number is unchanged.

solution_steps.text: β⁻ decay: n → p + e⁻ + \( \bar{\nu}_e \). Atomic number increases by 1 (one more proton). Mass number unchanged.

problems.question_html: Which type of radiation is most penetrating?

hints.text: Compare alpha (stopped by paper), beta (stopped by aluminum), gamma (stopped by ...).
Gamma radiation is most penetrating — it requires thick lead or concrete to stop. Alpha is least penetrating (stopped by paper).

solution_steps.text: Penetration order: alpha (least) < beta < gamma (most). Gamma rays require thick lead or concrete shielding.

problems.question_html: A sample of a radioactive isotope has a half-life of 10 days. After 30 days, what fraction of the original sample remains?

hints.text: How many half-lives fit in 30 days?
30 days = 3 half-lives. Remaining: \( (1/2)^3 = 1/8 \) of the original.

problems.question_html: Radium-226 undergoes alpha decay. What is the daughter nucleus?

hints.text: Alpha decay: mass number −4, atomic number −2. Radium is Z = 88.

problems.question_html: Carbon-14 undergoes β⁻ decay. What is the daughter nucleus?

hints.text: β⁻ decay: atomic number +1, mass number unchanged. Carbon is Z = 6.
\( ^{14}_6\text{C} \to ^{14}_7\text{N} + e^- + \bar{\nu}_e \). Z = 7 is Nitrogen.
